Hundreds of guests attended the annual awards banquet.
A formal banquet followed the graduation ceremony.

senses.definition: Noun: an elaborate or abundant meal served to many people.
examples: The guests enjoyed a banquet of roasted meats, vegetables, and desserts.
The royal banquet lasted several hours.
The tables were prepared for a lavish banquet.

senses.definition: Verb: to entertain someone with a large or formal feast.
examples: The visiting diplomats were banqueted at the palace.
The city banqueted the returning athletes.
The delegation was banqueted by local officials.

senses.definition: Verb: to attend or take part in a banquet or elaborate feast.
examples: The guests banqueted late into the evening.
They banqueted together after the ceremony.
The victorious officers banqueted in the great hall.

baptize.etymology: From Middle English baptisen, through Old French and Late Latin, from Greek baptizein, meaning to immerse, dip, or wash
baptize.explanation: Means to perform the Christian rite of baptism on a person, typically using water as a symbol of religious initiation, purification, or commitment. The word can also mean to give someone a name during baptism or, more broadly, to name or designate something.

senses.definition: To perform the Christian rite of baptism on a person by applying, pouring, or immersing the person in water.
examples: The minister baptized the child during the Sunday service.
Several new members were baptized in the river.
She decided to be baptized after joining the church.

senses.definition: To formally admit or initiate someone into the Christian faith through baptism.
examples: The converts were baptized into the church.
He was baptized as a young adult.
The congregation welcomed those who had recently been baptized.

senses.definition: To give a person a name during the ceremony of baptism.
examples: The child was baptized Michael.
She was baptized with the name Elizabeth.
According to the record, he was baptized John shortly after his birth.

senses.definition: Figurative: to give a name or designation to something.
examples: The explorers baptized the newly discovered landmark with a local name.
The new vessel was ceremonially baptized before its first voyage.
Residents jokingly baptized the unusually steep hill with a memorable nickname.

bar.etymology: From Middle English barre, from Old French barre, ultimately from Late Latin barra, meaning a bar, rod, or barrier
bar.explanation: A highly versatile word referring to a long rigid piece of material, a barrier or obstruction, a counter or establishment where drinks are served, a measured section of music, or the legal profession. As a verb, bar means to block, exclude, or prohibit. The word is also used as a unit of pressure and as a preposition meaning except for.

senses.definition: Noun: a long, narrow, rigid piece of metal, wood, or another solid material.
examples: The gate was secured with a heavy metal bar.
He lifted the weight by gripping the bar.
Steel bars reinforced the structure.

senses.definition: Noun: something that blocks, prevents, or restricts movement, access, or progress.
examples: The locked gate formed a bar to further entry.
Lack of funding became a bar to completing the project.
The new requirement could create a bar to participation.

senses.definition: Noun: a counter at which alcoholic or other beverages are prepared and served.
examples: They ordered their drinks at the bar.
She sat at the bar while waiting for her friends.
The restaurant has a small bar near the entrance.

senses.definition: Noun: an establishment or room where alcoholic beverages are served, often along with food or entertainment.
examples: They met at a neighborhood bar after work.
The hotel has a bar on the ground floor.
A jazz band performs at the bar on weekends.

senses.definition: Noun: a quantity of a substance formed into a long or rectangular solid piece.
examples: She bought a bar of chocolate.
There was a fresh bar of soap beside the sink.
The gold was formed into a solid bar.

senses.definition: Noun: one of the equal sections into which written music is divided by vertical lines.
examples: The melody begins in the fourth bar.
The musician repeated the final two bars.
Each bar contains a specific number of beats.

senses.definition: Noun: the legal profession collectively, especially lawyers who are qualified to practice law.
examples: She was admitted to the bar after passing the required examination.
He has been a member of the bar for twenty years.
The state bar establishes professional standards for attorneys.

senses.definition: Noun: a unit of pressure equal to 100,000 pascals.
examples: The pressure was measured at two bar.
The equipment operates at a pressure of several bar.
Engineers monitored the pressure gauge in bar.

senses.definition: Verb: to block or prevent passage through or into a place.
examples: A fallen tree barred the road.
Security officers barred the entrance.
Heavy furniture barred the doorway.

senses.definition: Verb: to officially prohibit, exclude, or prevent someone or something from participating or occurring.
examples: The rules bar employees from accepting certain gifts.
He was barred from entering the building.
The law bars companies from using the information for that purpose.

senses.definition: Preposition: except for or excluding a particular person or thing.
examples: Everyone bar one student completed the assignment.
The museum is open every day bar Monday.
All of the proposals, bar one, were approved.

barbecue.etymology: From Spanish barbacoa, borrowed from an Indigenous Caribbean language, referring originally to a wooden framework used for cooking, drying, or sleeping
barbecue.explanation: Refers to a method of cooking food, especially meat, over or near an open flame, hot coals, or another source of heat. It can also refer to the equipment used for this cooking, the food itself, or a social gathering centered on grilled or smoked food. As a verb, barbecue means to cook food in this manner.

senses.definition: Noun: a method of cooking food, especially meat, slowly or directly over fire, hot coals, or another source of heat.
examples: Barbecue is a popular method of cooking meat outdoors.
The restaurant specializes in slow-cooked barbecue.
Different regions have developed distinct styles of barbecue.

senses.definition: Noun: meat or other food prepared by barbecuing, often with seasoning, smoke, or sauce.
examples: We ordered barbecue with beans and coleslaw.
The restaurant serves several kinds of barbecue.
He prepared enough barbecue to feed the entire family.

senses.definition: Noun: an outdoor grill, pit, or other piece of equipment used for cooking food over heat.
examples: He cleaned the barbecue before cooking dinner.
They bought a new barbecue for the patio.
The public park has several barbecues available for visitors.

senses.definition: Noun: an outdoor meal, party, or social gathering at which food is grilled or smoked.
examples: The neighbors held a barbecue in their backyard.
We were invited to a barbecue on Saturday.
The company organized a summer barbecue for its employees.

senses.definition: Verb: to cook food, especially meat, over or near fire, hot coals, or another source of heat.
examples: They barbecued chicken for dinner.
He spent the afternoon barbecuing ribs.
We plan to barbecue vegetables and burgers outside.

barber.etymology: From Middle English barbour, from Anglo-French barbour, ultimately from Latin barba, meaning beard
barber.explanation: Refers to a person whose occupation involves cutting and grooming hair, especially men's hair, and traditionally shaving or trimming beards. As a verb, barber means to cut, trim, or groom someone's hair or beard.

senses.definition: Noun: a person whose occupation is cutting, trimming, styling, or grooming hair, especially men's hair.
examples: The barber trimmed his hair and beard.
She works as a barber at a neighborhood shop.
He visits the same barber every month.

senses.definition: Noun: traditionally, a person who also shaves or trims customers' facial hair.
examples: The barber carefully shaped his beard.
He asked the barber for a shave.
The shop offers traditional barber services such as haircuts and beard trimming.

senses.definition: Verb: to cut, trim, shave, or otherwise groom a person's hair or beard.
examples: He barbered his son's hair at home.
The stylist carefully barbered the edges of his beard.
He learned to barber professionally after completing his training.

bare.etymology: From Old English bær, meaning uncovered, naked, or lacking a covering
bare.explanation: Describes something that is uncovered, exposed, empty, plain, or reduced to only what is necessary. As a verb, bare means to uncover, expose, or reveal something.

senses.definition: Adjective: not covered by clothing, material, or another protective layer.
examples: She walked across the beach in bare feet.
His bare arms were exposed to the cold air.
The wires should not be handled with bare hands.

senses.definition: Adjective: lacking the usual covering, vegetation, furnishings, or decoration.
examples: The trees were bare during the winter.
The apartment was almost bare when they moved in.
The fire left the hillside bare.

senses.definition: Adjective: containing only what is essential or strictly necessary.
examples: They survived with only the bare necessities.
The report gave the bare facts of the case.
The project was completed with the bare minimum of equipment.

senses.definition: Adjective: openly exposed, visible, or revealed.
examples: The storm exposed bare rock beneath the soil.
The investigation laid the facts bare.
The damaged wall revealed bare brick underneath.

senses.definition: Verb: to uncover, expose, or reveal something.
examples: He bared his arm for the injection.
The dog bared its teeth at the stranger.
The documents bared serious problems within the organization.

barely.etymology: Formed from bare with the adverb-forming suffix -ly, originally conveying the sense of plainly, openly, or with nothing extra, and later developing the common meaning of only just or scarcely
barely.explanation: Means only just, scarcely, or by a very small amount. It is commonly used to indicate that something almost did not happen, exist, qualify, or reach a particular level.

senses.definition: Only just; by the smallest or narrowest amount.
examples: She barely passed the examination.
The car barely fit into the parking space.
He barely caught the train before it departed.

senses.definition: Hardly or scarcely; almost not at all.
examples: I could barely hear him over the noise.
She was so tired that she could barely keep her eyes open.
The writing was barely visible in the dim light.

senses.definition: Only a short time before or after something happened.
examples: They had barely arrived when the storm began.
She had barely finished speaking before the audience applauded.
The meeting had barely started when the fire alarm sounded.

bargain.etymology: From Middle English bargayn, from Old French bargaignier, meaning to negotiate, haggle, or make an agreement
bargain.explanation: Refers to an agreement reached between parties, especially concerning a price or exchange. It can also mean something bought for less than its usual or expected value. As a verb, bargain means to negotiate the terms of an agreement, especially the price.

senses.definition: Noun: an agreement between two or more parties concerning what each will do, provide, or accept.
examples: They made a bargain to divide the work equally.
The agreement was more favorable than the original bargain.
Both sides were expected to honor their bargain.

senses.definition: Noun: something purchased at a price lower than its usual, expected, or perceived value.
examples: The coat was a bargain at half the regular price.
She found several bargains at the sale.
The used car turned out to be a real bargain.

senses.definition: Verb: to negotiate the price, terms, or conditions of an agreement.
examples: They bargained with the seller over the price.
The union bargained for higher wages.
She spent several minutes bargaining at the market.

senses.definition: Verb: to expect, anticipate, or make plans on the basis of a particular outcome, especially in the phrase bargain for.
examples: We had not bargained for such heavy traffic.
The company received more demand than it had bargained for.
He got more responsibility than he had bargained for.

bark.etymology: The sense referring to a dog's sound comes from Old English beorcan, meaning to bark. The sense referring to the outer covering of a tree comes from Old Norse bǫrkr, meaning bark or rind.
bark.explanation: Refers either to the short, sharp sound made by a dog or certain other animals, or to the tough outer covering of a tree or woody plant. As a verb, bark means to make such a sound, to speak sharply, or to remove bark from a tree.

senses.definition: Noun: the short, sharp sound made by a dog or certain other animals.
examples: We heard the dog's bark from across the street.
A loud bark came from behind the fence.
The puppy's bark was surprisingly deep.

senses.definition: Verb: to make the characteristic short, sharp sound of a dog.
examples: The dog barked when someone knocked at the door.
Several dogs began barking at once.
The puppy barked excitedly at the visitor.

senses.definition: Verb: to speak or shout in a sharp, abrupt, or commanding manner.
examples: The officer barked an order to the soldiers.
She barked instructions across the crowded room.
He barked at everyone to move quickly.

senses.definition: Noun: the tough outer covering of the trunk, branches, and roots of a tree or other woody plant.
examples: The bark of the tree was rough and deeply grooved.
Insects were hiding beneath the bark.
The deer had rubbed some of the bark from the trunk.

senses.definition: Verb: to remove or damage the bark of a tree or piece of wood.
examples: Workers barked the logs before processing them.
The machine is designed to bark timber quickly.
Animals had barked several young trees by chewing on them.

barley.etymology: From Old English bærlic, referring to barley, one of the oldest cultivated cereal grains
barley.explanation: Refers to a cereal grain grown for food, animal feed, and the production of beverages such as beer and whisky. The word can refer either to the barley plant itself or to its edible grains.

senses.definition: A cereal plant cultivated for its edible grain.
examples: The farmer planted barley in the spring.
Barley grows well in relatively cool climates.
Fields of barley stretched across the valley.

senses.definition: The grain produced by the barley plant, used as food, animal feed, and an ingredient in various products.
examples: She added barley to the vegetable soup.
The livestock were fed a mixture containing barley.
Pearled barley is commonly used in soups and stews.

senses.definition: Barley grain used in malting and the production of alcoholic beverages such as beer and whisky.
examples: The brewery uses malted barley to make beer.
Barley is an important ingredient in many types of whisky.
The harvested barley was sent to a malt house for processing.

barn.etymology: From Old English bereærn, formed from bere, meaning barley, and ærn, meaning house or building, originally referring to a building used for storing grain
barn.explanation: Refers to a large farm building used for storing crops, hay, equipment, or housing livestock. The word can also describe a large, plain building that resembles a traditional farm barn.

senses.definition: A large farm building used to store hay, grain, equipment, or other agricultural materials.
examples: The farmer stored the hay in the barn.
Several tractors were parked inside the barn.
The old barn stood beside the wheat field.

senses.definition: A farm building used to shelter livestock.
examples: The horses were brought into the barn before the storm.
The cows returned to the barn in the evening.
The barn contained stalls for several animals.

senses.definition: Informal: a very large, plain, or spacious building or room resembling a barn.
examples: The warehouse was a huge barn of a building.
The empty hall felt like a barn.
They converted the barnlike structure into an event space.

barrel.etymology: From Middle English barel, from Old French baril, referring to a cylindrical wooden container used for storing or transporting liquids and other goods
barrel.explanation: Refers primarily to a large cylindrical container, traditionally made of wooden staves and used for storing liquids or other materials. It can also mean the cylindrical tube of a firearm, a standard unit used to measure certain commodities, or, as a verb, to move rapidly and forcefully.

senses.definition: Noun: a large cylindrical container, traditionally made of wooden staves, used for storing or transporting liquids or other materials.
examples: The winery stored the wine in oak barrels.
Workers rolled the barrel into the warehouse.
Rainwater collected in a large barrel beside the house.

senses.definition: Noun: the long cylindrical tube of a firearm through which a projectile travels when fired.
examples: The barrel of the rifle was pointed toward the ground.
The technician inspected the firearm's barrel for damage.
Residue had accumulated inside the barrel.

senses.definition: Noun: a unit of volume used for measuring commodities, especially petroleum, with the exact quantity depending on the substance and system of measurement.
examples: Oil prices are often quoted by the barrel.
The field produces thousands of barrels of petroleum each day.
The company reported its output in barrels.

senses.definition: Noun: a cylindrical or barrel-shaped part of a machine, instrument, or other object.
examples: The key fits into the lock barrel.
The lens barrel protects several internal components.
The machine uses a rotating barrel to mix the material.

senses.definition: Verb: to move very quickly, often with considerable force or little caution.
examples: The truck barreled down the highway.
The children barreled through the doorway.
The storm barreled toward the coast.

barren.etymology: From Middle English barein, from Old French baraine, referring to land or a living thing that does not produce or bear fruit
barren.explanation: Describes land that is unable to support much vegetation or produce crops, or something that produces little or nothing useful. Figuratively, it can describe a place, period, idea, or effort lacking growth, results, creativity, or meaningful content.

senses.definition: Unable to support much vegetation or produce crops.
examples: The barren soil could support only a few hardy plants.
Years of drought left the fields barren.
The travelers crossed a barren stretch of desert.

senses.definition: Lacking vegetation, life, or other signs of natural abundance.
examples: The rocky island appeared barren from a distance.
The landscape was cold and barren.
Only a few shrubs grew on the barren hillside.

senses.definition: Producing little or nothing useful, successful, or worthwhile.
examples: Months of negotiation proved barren.
The search produced a barren set of results.
Their efforts were largely barren until new evidence appeared.

senses.definition: Lacking ideas, creativity, interest, or meaningful content.
examples: Critics described the proposal as intellectually barren.
The discussion became barren once everyone stopped offering new ideas.
He struggled through a barren period in his writing career.

senses.definition: Unable to reproduce or produce offspring, especially in older or technical usage.
examples: The farmer believed the animal was barren.
Older agricultural texts sometimes describe infertile livestock as barren.
The term barren has historically been used for animals unable to reproduce.

barrier.etymology: From Middle English barrere, from Old French barriere, meaning a fence, gate, or obstacle, derived from barre, meaning bar
barrier.explanation: Refers to something that blocks, separates, protects, or prevents movement, access, communication, or progress. A barrier may be a physical structure or a figurative obstacle such as cost, language, discrimination, or lack of information.

senses.definition: A physical structure or object that blocks passage, separates areas, or restricts movement.
examples: Workers placed a barrier across the road.
A concrete barrier separated the two lanes of traffic.
The fence formed a barrier around the construction site.

senses.definition: Something that prevents or makes progress, communication, participation, or achievement more difficult.
examples: High tuition can be a barrier to education.
Language differences created a barrier to communication.
The organization worked to remove barriers to employment.

senses.definition: Something that protects a person, place, or thing by preventing harmful substances, forces, or conditions from reaching it.
examples: The wall provides a barrier against the wind.
Protective clothing creates a barrier between the skin and hazardous materials.
The coastal wetlands form a natural barrier against storm waves.

senses.definition: A boundary or dividing feature that separates one area, group, condition, or system from another.
examples: The mountain range forms a natural barrier between the regions.
The membrane acts as a barrier between the cell and its surroundings.
Social barriers once sharply separated the two communities.

base.etymology: From Middle English and Old French base, ultimately from Latin basis and Greek basis, meaning a step, pedestal, or foundation
base.explanation: Refers to the bottom or supporting part of something, a main location from which activities are conducted, or the underlying foundation of an idea or system. It also has specialized meanings in sports, mathematics, chemistry, and the military. As a verb, base means to establish or locate something somewhere or to use something as the foundation for a conclusion or action.

senses.definition: Noun: the lowest or supporting part of an object or structure.
examples: The lamp has a heavy metal base.
The statue stands on a stone base.
Cracks appeared near the base of the wall.

senses.definition: Noun: the bottom or lowest part of something, especially a natural feature.
examples: They camped near the base of the mountain.
A trail begins at the base of the hill.
Snow had accumulated around the base of the tree.

senses.definition: Noun: a place from which an organization, group, or operation conducts its main activities.
examples: The city serves as the company's regional base.
The researchers established a base near the study area.
The campaign opened a new base of operations downtown.

senses.definition: Noun: a military installation from which personnel, aircraft, ships, or other operations are supported.
examples: The aircraft returned to the military base.
Thousands of personnel are stationed at the base.
The naval base supports ships operating in the region.

senses.definition: Noun: the underlying foundation, principle, or source from which something develops.
examples: Trust forms the base of a strong relationship.
The company built a broad customer base.
Scientific evidence provided the base for the new theory.

senses.definition: Noun: in baseball and related games, one of the designated positions that a runner must reach in order to score.
examples: The runner reached second base safely.
She slid into base before the tag.
The batter drove in a runner from third base.

senses.definition: Noun: in mathematics, the number used as the foundation of a numeral system or as the repeated factor in an exponential expression.
examples: The decimal system uses base ten.
Binary numbers are written in base two.
In the expression two cubed, two is the base.

senses.definition: Noun: in chemistry, a substance that can accept hydrogen ions or react with an acid to form a salt and, often, water.
examples: Sodium hydroxide is a strong base.
The acid reacted with the base.
The laboratory exercise compared several acids and bases.

senses.definition: Verb: to use something as the foundation, evidence, or starting point for a decision, judgment, or creation.
examples: The report is based on data collected over five years.
She based her decision on the available evidence.
The film was based on a historical event.

senses.definition: Verb: to locate or establish a person, organization, or operation in a particular place.
examples: The company is based in Seattle.
The research team based its operations near the coast.
Several aircraft are based at the regional airport.

senses.definition: Adjective: lacking higher moral qualities; dishonorable, selfish, or contemptible.
examples: The betrayal was motivated by base greed.
He rejected such base motives.
The character's base behavior eventually caused his downfall.

baseball.etymology: Formed from base and ball, referring to a game in which players advance around a series of bases after striking a ball
baseball.explanation: Refers to a team sport in which players take turns batting a ball and attempting to score runs by advancing around four bases while the opposing team tries to record outs. The word can also refer to the ball used to play the game.

senses.definition: A team sport in which a player strikes a pitched ball with a bat and attempts to score runs by advancing around four bases.
examples: The children played baseball at the park.
He began playing baseball when he was eight years old.
Baseball games are divided into innings.

senses.definition: The organized sport of baseball, including its teams, leagues, players, rules, and competitions.
examples: She has followed professional baseball for many years.
Baseball became an important part of American popular culture.
He hopes to pursue a career in baseball.

senses.definition: The small, hard ball used in the game of baseball, consisting of a core wrapped in material and covered with stitched leather or a similar covering.
examples: The pitcher threw the baseball toward home plate.
A baseball landed in the stands.
The child brought a glove and a baseball to the field.

basement.etymology: Formed from base with the suffix -ment, referring to the lowest or foundational part of a building
basement.explanation: Refers to a floor or level of a building that is wholly or partly below ground level. Basements are commonly used for storage, utilities, living space, workshops, or other purposes.

senses.definition: A floor or level of a building located wholly or partly below ground level.
examples: The house has a finished basement.
They stored old furniture in the basement.
The basement windows are just above ground level.

senses.definition: A below-ground area of a building used for storage, mechanical equipment, work, recreation, or living space.
examples: The furnace is located in the basement.
They converted the basement into a family room.
His workshop occupies one side of the basement.

basic.etymology: Formed from base with the suffix -ic, ultimately from Greek basis, meaning foundation or starting point
basic.explanation: Describes something that forms the foundation or essential part of a subject, system, activity, or need. It can also mean simple, introductory, or lacking additional features. As a noun, basic can refer to a fundamental principle, skill, requirement, or element.

senses.definition: Adjective: forming the foundation, essential part, or starting point of something.
examples: Students first learn the basic principles of mathematics.
Food and shelter are basic human needs.
The course introduces the basic concepts of biology.

senses.definition: Adjective: simple or introductory rather than advanced or complicated.
examples: She has a basic understanding of computer programming.
The manual provides basic instructions for operating the machine.
He enrolled in a basic Spanish course.

senses.definition: Adjective: containing only the standard or essential features, without additional improvements or luxuries.
examples: The hotel room was basic but comfortable.
The basic model does not include heated seats.
They purchased the basic version of the software.

senses.definition: Noun: a fundamental principle, skill, requirement, or element.
examples: The instructor began by reviewing the basics.
You should master the basics before attempting advanced techniques.
The course teaches the basics of financial management.

senses.definition: Adjective: in chemistry, having the properties of a base or having a pH greater than 7.
examples: The solution became basic after the chemical was added.
Soap is generally basic rather than acidic.
The students tested whether the liquid was acidic or basic.

basically.etymology: Formed from basic with the adverb-forming suffix -ally, meaning in a fundamental, essential, or simple manner
basically.explanation: Means in the most important, fundamental, or essential respects. It is also commonly used to introduce a simplified explanation or summary of a more complicated situation.

senses.definition: In the most important, fundamental, or essential respects.
examples: The two proposals are basically the same.
The machine is basically a more powerful version of the older model.
Their goals remained basically unchanged.

senses.definition: Used to give a simple explanation or summary of something more complicated.
examples: Basically, the system collects information and organizes it into categories.
Basically, we need to finish the work before Friday.
The process is basically a series of repeated steps.

senses.definition: For the most part; generally or approximately, though not necessarily in every detail.
examples: The building is basically complete.
Everyone was basically satisfied with the result.
The plan worked basically as expected.

basin.etymology: From Middle English basin, from Old French bacin, referring to a broad, shallow vessel or container
basin.explanation: Refers to a broad, usually rounded container used to hold water or other liquids. It can also describe a natural or artificial depression in the land, especially an area drained by a river and its tributaries.

senses.definition: A broad, usually shallow container used for holding water or other liquids.
examples: She filled the basin with warm water.
The nurse placed a basin beside the bed.
He washed his hands in a small metal basin.

senses.definition: A bowl-shaped fixture used for washing, especially a sink or washbasin.
examples: Water collected in the bathroom basin.
The plumber replaced the cracked basin.
She cleaned the ceramic basin with soap.

senses.definition: A low area of land surrounded by higher ground.
examples: The city lies in a broad mountain basin.
Sediment accumulated at the bottom of the basin.
The desert basin receives very little rainfall.

senses.definition: An area of land drained by a river and all of its tributaries.
examples: The river basin covers several states.
Heavy rain throughout the basin caused the river to rise.
Scientists studied water use across the entire drainage basin.

senses.definition: A large natural or artificial area that holds or collects water.
examples: The harbor basin was dredged to accommodate larger ships.
A retention basin collects runoff after heavy storms.
Engineers designed the basin to store excess water.

basis.etymology: From Latin basis, from Greek basis, meaning a step, pedestal, foundation, or that on which something rests
basis.explanation: Refers to the underlying foundation, principle, reason, or set of facts on which something is built, established, judged, or explained. It can also describe the method or regular arrangement according to which something occurs.
usageNotes: The plural of basis is bases, pronounced BAY-seez. This spelling is also the plural of base, but the two plurals are pronounced differently.

senses.definition: The underlying foundation, principle, or idea on which something is established or developed.
examples: Trust is the basis of a strong partnership.
The Constitution provides the legal basis for the government's authority.
Scientific observation formed the basis of the theory.

senses.definition: A reason, fact, or set of circumstances used to justify a decision, belief, judgment, or action.
examples: There was no basis for the accusation.
The committee made its decision on the basis of the available evidence.
The court found a sufficient basis for further review.

senses.definition: A particular method, arrangement, or system according to which something is done or organized.
examples: Employees are paid on a weekly basis.
The committee meets on a regular basis.
The service is provided on a voluntary basis.

senses.definition: The fundamental relationship or condition used for comparison, calculation, or evaluation.
examples: The figures were adjusted to provide a fair basis for comparison.
Costs are calculated on a per-person basis.
The two proposals were evaluated on the same basis.

basket.etymology: From Middle English basket, probably from an Old North French or related Romance source referring to a woven container
basket.explanation: Refers primarily to a container made from woven, interlaced, or flexible material and used for carrying or storing objects. In basketball, it can also mean the hoop and net through which the ball is thrown or a successful score. As a verb, basket can mean to place or collect something in a basket.

senses.definition: Noun: a container made from woven or interlaced material, often with one or more handles, used for carrying or storing things.
examples: She carried the fruit in a wicker basket.
The laundry basket was full of clean clothes.
He placed the vegetables in a large basket.

senses.definition: Noun: the raised hoop and attached net used as the scoring target in basketball.
examples: The ball bounced off the rim of the basket.
He drove toward the basket for an easy shot.
The basket is mounted above the court.

senses.definition: Noun: a successful score in basketball made by throwing the ball through the hoop.
examples: She scored the winning basket.
The player made three baskets in the final minute.
His first basket gave the team an early lead.

senses.definition: Noun: a collection or group of goods, investments, currencies, or other items considered together.
examples: The index tracks a basket of major stocks.
The measure is based on the cost of a basket of consumer goods.
Investors compared the performance of several baskets of assets.

senses.definition: Verb: to place, gather, or carry something in a basket.
examples: Workers basketed the harvested fruit.
She basketed the clean towels for transport.
The produce was basketed before being taken to market.

basketball.etymology: Formed from basket and ball. The sport was invented in 1891 by James Naismith, whose original game used peach baskets as goals.
basketball.explanation: Refers to a team sport in which players attempt to score points by throwing a ball through an elevated hoop and net while preventing the opposing team from doing the same. The word can also refer to the ball used to play the sport.

senses.definition: A team sport in which players score points by throwing a ball through an elevated hoop and net.
examples: The students played basketball after school.
She joined the basketball team during her freshman year.
Basketball requires passing, shooting, dribbling, and defensive skills.

senses.definition: The organized sport of basketball, including its teams, leagues, players, rules, and competitions.
examples: He has followed professional basketball for many years.
Basketball is played competitively in countries around the world.
She hopes to pursue a career in basketball.

senses.definition: The inflated spherical ball used in the game of basketball.
examples: He bounced the basketball across the court.
She picked up a basketball and practiced shooting.
The coach placed several basketballs beside the court.

bass.etymology: Bass meaning a type of fish comes from Old English bærs. Bass meaning a low musical tone or register developed through forms related to Italian basso, meaning low. The two meanings have different historical origins and different pronunciations.
bass.explanation: Bass has two principal pronunciations and several meanings. Pronounced BASS, it refers to any of several kinds of freshwater or marine fish. Pronounced BAYSS, it refers to low musical tones, the lowest vocal or instrumental range, or instruments designed to produce low-pitched sounds.
usageNotes: Bass is a heteronym: the fish is pronounced BASS, while the musical word is pronounced BAYSS.

senses.definition: Noun, pronounced BASS: any of several freshwater or marine fish, many of which are commonly caught for food or sport.
examples: He caught a large bass in the lake.
The river contains several species of bass.
They spent the morning fishing for bass.

senses.definition: Noun, pronounced BAYSS: the lowest range of musical tones or frequencies.
examples: The song has a powerful bass.
She increased the bass on the stereo.
The bass became stronger during the final section of the music.

senses.definition: Noun, pronounced BAYSS: the lowest adult male singing voice or a singer who has such a voice.
examples: He sings bass in the choir.
The bass performed the lowest notes of the harmony.
The choir includes two tenors and two basses.

senses.definition: Noun, pronounced BAYSS: an instrument that produces the low-pitched part of a musical arrangement, especially a bass guitar or double bass.
examples: She plays bass in a jazz band.
The bass provides the foundation of the rhythm section.
He switched from guitar to bass.

senses.definition: Adjective, pronounced BAYSS: relating to or producing low musical tones.
examples: The song begins with a bass note.
A bass speaker reproduces low frequencies.
He practiced the bass part before rehearsal.

bat.etymology: The word has separate historical origins for its major meanings. Bat meaning a striking implement developed from Middle English forms referring to a club or stick. Bat meaning the flying mammal developed from a different Middle English word and replaced older English names for the animal.
bat.explanation: Refers either to a flying mammal with wings formed from stretched skin or to a club-shaped implement used to strike a ball in sports such as baseball and cricket. As a verb, bat means to strike something with a bat or to take a turn hitting in certain sports.

senses.definition: Noun: a nocturnal flying mammal with wings formed by a membrane of skin stretched between elongated fingers and the body.
examples: A bat flew out of the cave at sunset.
Many bats feed on insects during the night.
The researchers studied a colony of bats.

senses.definition: Noun: a club-shaped piece of equipment used for striking a ball in sports such as baseball or cricket.
examples: He swung the bat and hit the ball.
She carried her baseball bat to the field.
The player selected a lighter bat.

senses.definition: Verb: to strike a ball with a bat.
examples: He batted the ball into the outfield.
She batted the pitch over the fence.
The player batted the ball toward third base.

senses.definition: Verb: to take a turn or position as the player attempting to hit the ball in baseball, cricket, or a similar sport.
examples: Our team will bat first.
She bats third in the lineup.
He batted several times during the game.

senses.definition: Verb: to strike, tap, or knock something lightly or repeatedly.
examples: The cat batted the toy across the floor.
She batted his hand away.
The kitten batted at the hanging string.

batch.etymology: From Middle English bache, probably related to bake, originally referring to the quantity of bread produced in one baking
batch.explanation: Refers to a group or quantity of things produced, processed, handled, or considered together. As a verb, batch means to arrange or process items together as a group.

senses.definition: Noun: a quantity of food or other material made or prepared at one time.
examples: She baked a batch of cookies.
The factory produced a new batch of paint.
They prepared a large batch of soup for the event.

senses.definition: Noun: a group or set of people, objects, records, or tasks handled together.
examples: The office processed a batch of applications.
A new batch of students arrived for orientation.
The system uploaded the files in batches.

senses.definition: Noun: a quantity of goods produced during one manufacturing or processing cycle.
examples: The defective batch was removed from the warehouse.
Each batch is tested before shipment.
The company recalled a batch of products.

senses.definition: Verb: to group or process items together rather than individually.
examples: The program batches similar requests together.
Workers batched the orders by destination.
The files were batched for overnight processing.

bath.etymology: From Old English bæth, referring to the act of washing or to water used for washing the body
bath.explanation: Refers to the act of washing or soaking the body in water, the water used for that purpose, or the container in which a person bathes. It can also refer to a special liquid treatment used for cleaning, heating, cooling, or processing something.

senses.definition: The act of washing or soaking the body in water.
examples: The child took a bath before bedtime.
She enjoyed a warm bath after work.
He needed a bath after working in the garden.

senses.definition: The water in which a person washes or soaks the body.
examples: She tested the temperature of the bath before getting in.
He added soap to the bath.
The bath was still warm.

senses.definition: A bathtub or other container used for washing or soaking the body.
examples: The bathroom has a large bath and a separate shower.
She filled the bath with warm water.
The old house still has its original cast-iron bath.

senses.definition: A liquid or other medium in which an object or substance is placed for cleaning, heating, cooling, treatment, or processing.
examples: The laboratory sample was placed in a heated water bath.
The metal parts were lowered into a chemical bath.
The container was cooled in an ice bath.

bathe.etymology: From Old English bathian, meaning to wash, bathe, or immerse in water, related to bath
bathe.explanation: Means to wash or soak the body in water, to wash part of the body or another object, or to immerse something in liquid. Figuratively, it can also mean to cover or surround something with light, warmth, or another quality.

senses.definition: To wash or soak one's body in water.
examples: She bathed before going to bed.
The children bathed after playing outside.
He prefers to bathe in the evening.

senses.definition: To wash a person, animal, or part of the body with water or another liquid.
examples: She gently bathed the baby's face.
The nurse bathed the wound with clean water.
He bathed the dog's muddy paws.

senses.definition: To immerse or soak something in a liquid.
examples: The cloth was bathed in warm water.
The vegetables were bathed in a light sauce.
The technician bathed the component in a cleaning solution.

senses.definition: To swim or spend time in a body of water, especially for recreation.
examples: Visitors bathed in the warm sea.
The family bathed in the lake during the afternoon.
Tourists were warned not to bathe near the strong current.

senses.definition: Figurative: to cover, surround, or fill something with light, warmth, or another quality.
examples: The setting sun bathed the mountains in golden light.
Moonlight bathed the garden in a pale glow.
Warm sunlight bathed the room.

bathroom.etymology: Formed from bath and room, originally referring to a room containing facilities for bathing
bathroom.explanation: Refers to a room containing a bathtub or shower and usually a toilet and sink. In American English, bathroom is also commonly used for any room containing a toilet, even if no bathing facilities are present.

senses.definition: A room containing a bathtub or shower and usually a toilet and sink.
examples: The house has two bathrooms.
She left her towel in the bathroom.
They renovated the bathroom and installed a new shower.

senses.definition: In American English, a room containing a toilet and sink, whether or not it includes bathing facilities.
examples: Excuse me, where is the bathroom?
The restaurant has a bathroom near the entrance.
He stopped at a gas station to use the bathroom.

baton.etymology: From French bâton, meaning stick, staff, or rod
baton.explanation: Refers to a short stick or rod used for a particular purpose, such as directing musicians, passing between runners in a relay race, serving as a symbol of authority, or functioning as a police impact weapon.

senses.definition: A thin stick used by a conductor to direct an orchestra, band, or other musical ensemble.
examples: The conductor raised her baton before the orchestra began.
He used the baton to indicate changes in tempo.
The musicians watched the conductor's baton carefully.

senses.definition: A short stick carried and passed between runners in a relay race.
examples: She passed the baton to the next runner.
The team practiced its baton exchanges before the race.
Dropping the baton cost the team valuable time.

senses.definition: A short, heavy stick carried by police officers or security personnel as an impact weapon.
examples: The officer carried a baton as part of his equipment.
Police training included instruction on the proper use of a baton.
The baton remained secured on the officer's belt.

senses.definition: A staff or rod carried as a symbol of office, rank, authority, or ceremonial position.
examples: The official carried a ceremonial baton during the procession.
The baton symbolized the commander's authority.
Historical portraits sometimes show military leaders holding batons.

senses.definition: A lightweight rod used by a drum major or majorette for signaling, marching, or performing routines.
examples: The majorette twirled the baton during the parade.
She practiced throwing and catching her baton.
The drum major raised the baton to signal the band.

batter.etymology: The verb comes from Middle English bater, from Old French batre, meaning to beat or strike. The cooking sense developed from the idea of ingredients being beaten together into a mixture.
batter.explanation: As a noun, batter can refer to a mixture of flour, liquid, and other ingredients used in cooking or to a player whose turn it is to hit the ball in sports such as baseball or cricket. As a verb, batter means to strike something repeatedly and forcefully or to damage it through repeated impact.

senses.definition: Noun: a mixture of flour, liquid, and usually other ingredients prepared for cooking or baking.
examples: She poured the pancake batter onto the hot griddle.
The cake batter should be mixed until smooth.
He dipped the fish in batter before frying it.

senses.definition: Noun: a player whose turn it is to attempt to hit the ball in baseball, softball, cricket, or a similar sport.
examples: The batter stepped up to the plate.
The pitcher struck out the next batter.
The batter hit the ball into left field.

senses.definition: Verb: to strike someone or something repeatedly and forcefully.
examples: Heavy waves battered the shoreline.
The storm battered the windows throughout the night.
Repeated impacts battered the old wooden door.

senses.definition: Verb: to damage, weaken, or wear down something through repeated force, pressure, or hardship.
examples: Years of storms had battered the building.
The economy was battered by a prolonged recession.
The coastline was badly battered by the hurricane.

senses.definition: Verb: to coat food in batter before cooking it.
examples: The cook battered the fish before placing it in the fryer.
She battered the vegetables and fried them until crisp.
The onion rings were freshly battered.

battery.etymology: From Middle French batterie, meaning a beating, attack, or bombardment, derived from battre, meaning to beat or strike. The electrical sense developed later from the idea of a connected group or series of devices.
battery.explanation: Refers most commonly to a device that stores chemical energy and supplies electrical power. The word also has specialized meanings in law, the military, and general usage, where it can describe unlawful physical contact, a group of artillery weapons, or a collection of similar things used together.

senses.definition: A device consisting of one or more electrochemical cells that stores energy and supplies electrical power.
examples: The flashlight needs a new battery.
She charged the battery before leaving home.
The car would not start because its battery was dead.

senses.definition: A rechargeable electrical power unit used in vehicles, computers, phones, tools, and other equipment.
examples: The phone battery lasted all day.
The electric vehicle has a large rechargeable battery.
He replaced the laptop battery after several years of use.

senses.definition: In law, intentional and unlawful physical contact with another person without consent or legal justification.
examples: The defendant was charged with battery after the altercation.
The lawsuit included an allegation of assault and battery.
The exact legal definition of battery varies by jurisdiction.

senses.definition: A military unit consisting of artillery weapons and the personnel who operate them.
examples: The artillery battery moved into position before dawn.
The battery opened fire on the enemy position.
Several guns formed part of the coastal defense battery.

senses.definition: A group, series, or collection of similar things used, performed, or considered together.
examples: The doctor ordered a battery of tests.
The researchers conducted a battery of experiments.
Applicants completed a battery of assessments.

battle.etymology: From Middle English bataille, from Old French bataille, ultimately from Late Latin battualia, referring to fighting or combat
battle.explanation: Refers to a fight or armed conflict between opposing forces, especially as part of a larger war. More broadly, it can describe any prolonged struggle, competition, or effort to overcome a difficult problem. As a verb, battle means to fight or struggle against an opponent, condition, or obstacle.

senses.definition: Noun: an armed fight between opposing military forces, usually within a larger war or campaign.
examples: The battle lasted for several hours.
Thousands of soldiers took part in the battle.
The army won an important battle during the campaign.

senses.definition: Noun: a prolonged struggle, contest, or effort against an opponent, problem, or difficult condition.
examples: The company faces a difficult battle for market share.
She won her battle against the unfair policy.
The community began a long battle to preserve the historic building.

senses.definition: Noun: a competition or contest between people, groups, ideas, or interests.
examples: The election became a close political battle.
The two companies are engaged in a battle for customers.
The debate turned into a battle over competing priorities.

senses.definition: Verb: to fight against an enemy or opponent.
examples: The soldiers battled through the night.
The two armies battled for control of the city.
The teams battled until the final seconds of the game.

senses.definition: Verb: to struggle persistently against a problem, condition, or obstacle.
examples: Firefighters battled the blaze for hours.
The organization is battling rising costs.
Farmers battled drought throughout the summer.

battlefield.etymology: Formed from battle and field, referring originally to an open area or field where opposing forces engage in combat
battlefield.explanation: Refers literally to a place where a battle is fought. Figuratively, it can also describe an area, issue, institution, or situation in which competing groups, ideas, or interests are engaged in intense conflict.

senses.definition: A place or area where opposing military forces fight a battle.
examples: The soldiers crossed the battlefield before dawn.
Thousands of artifacts have been recovered from the historic battlefield.
Medical teams treated wounded soldiers near the battlefield.

senses.definition: A former site of military combat, especially one preserved or studied for its historical significance.
examples: The battlefield is now protected as a historic site.
Visitors toured the Civil War battlefield.
Archaeologists examined the battlefield for evidence of troop movements.

senses.definition: Figurative: a setting or issue in which opposing groups, ideas, interests, or forces compete intensely.
examples: Education became a political battlefield during the campaign.
The courtroom turned into a battlefield over competing interpretations of the law.
Social media has become a major battlefield for public opinion.

bay.etymology: The word has several historical origins. Bay meaning a coastal inlet comes through Old French baie. Bay meaning a compartment or recessed area is related to architectural uses of the word. Bay meaning a reddish-brown color comes from Old French bai, while the verb meaning to howl developed from a separate Old French source.
bay.explanation: Refers most commonly to a broad inlet of the sea or another body of water. It can also mean a defined compartment or recessed area in a building, vehicle, or structure. Bay additionally describes a reddish-brown horse or color, and as a verb can mean to howl or cry loudly, especially of dogs or hounds.

senses.definition: Noun: a broad inlet of the sea, lake, or other body of water where the land curves inward.
examples: The boat anchored in a quiet bay.
The city overlooks a large bay.
Several small islands lie near the entrance to the bay.

senses.definition: Noun: a distinct compartment, section, or recessed area in a building or structure.
examples: The truck pulled into the loading bay.
The mechanic worked in the third repair bay.
Emergency vehicles were parked in separate bays.

senses.definition: Noun: a section or compartment designed to hold equipment, cargo, or machinery.
examples: The aircraft has a large cargo bay.
The computer case contains several drive bays.
The spacecraft's payload bay opened in orbit.

senses.definition: Noun: a reddish-brown horse with a black mane, tail, and lower legs.
examples: She rode a bay across the field.
The stable housed two chestnuts and a bay.
The bay won the final race of the afternoon.

senses.definition: Adjective: reddish-brown in color, especially when describing a horse.
examples: He purchased a bay mare.
The bay horse had a black mane and tail.
A bay stallion stood near the fence.

senses.definition: Noun: a prolonged, deep cry or howl, especially that of a dog or hound.
examples: The bay of the hounds echoed through the woods.
They heard a distant bay in the night.
The dog's bay carried across the valley.

senses.definition: Verb: to howl or cry loudly and repeatedly, especially like a hound.
examples: The hounds bayed throughout the night.
Dogs bayed at the approaching stranger.
The pack began baying when it detected the scent.

beach.etymology: From Middle English beche, probably referring originally to the pebbly or sandy shore of a body of water
beach.explanation: Refers to an area of sand, pebbles, or other loose material along the edge of an ocean, lake, or other body of water. As a verb, beach means to bring or run a boat, ship, or marine animal onto the shore.

senses.definition: Noun: an area of sand, pebbles, or other loose material along the shore of an ocean, lake, or other body of water.
examples: The children played on the beach.
They walked along the beach at sunset.
Waves washed shells onto the beach.

senses.definition: Noun: a coastal area used for swimming, recreation, or other activities near the water.
examples: The beach was crowded on the warm summer afternoon.
They spent the weekend relaxing at the beach.
Lifeguards watched swimmers from the beach.

senses.definition: Verb: to bring or run a boat or ship onto the shore.
examples: The crew beached the small boat above the tide line.
They beached the canoe before setting up camp.
The damaged vessel was deliberately beached for repairs.

senses.definition: Verb: to come or become stranded on a shore, especially of a marine animal or vessel.
examples: Several whales beached along the coastline.
The storm caused the fishing boat to beach on a sandbar.
Rescuers worked to return the beached dolphin to deeper water.

bead.etymology: From Old English gebed, meaning prayer. The word came to refer to the small objects used for counting prayers and later broadened to mean small rounded decorative objects
bead.explanation: Refers primarily to a small rounded object, often made of glass, wood, stone, metal, or plastic, with a hole through it for threading onto jewelry or decorative work. It can also mean a small rounded drop of liquid. As a verb, bead means to form into small rounded drops or to decorate with beads.

senses.definition: Noun: a small rounded object, usually with a hole through the center, used in jewelry, decoration, or craftwork.
examples: She threaded each bead onto the string.
The necklace was made from colorful glass beads.
One bead fell from the bracelet.

senses.definition: Noun: a small rounded drop of liquid.
examples: A bead of sweat formed on his forehead.
Beads of water covered the cold glass.
A single bead of rain rolled down the window.

senses.definition: Noun: a small rounded projection, ridge, or line formed on a surface, especially in manufacturing or construction.
examples: The welder laid a smooth bead along the joint.
A bead of sealant was applied around the window.
The carpenter added a decorative bead to the edge of the panel.

senses.definition: Verb: to form or gather into small rounded drops.
examples: Water beaded on the waxed surface.
Sweat beaded on her forehead.
Rain began to bead on the windshield.

senses.definition: Verb: to decorate or cover something with beads.
examples: She beaded the fabric by hand.
The costume was carefully beaded with small crystals.
He learned how to bead traditional patterns onto leather.

beak.etymology: From Middle English bec, from Old French bec, meaning the bill or projecting mouthpart of a bird
beak.explanation: Refers primarily to the hard, projecting mouthpart of a bird, used for eating, grooming, defense, and other activities. The word can also describe a similar projecting structure in certain other animals or objects.

senses.definition: The hard, projecting mouthpart of a bird, consisting of the upper and lower jaws covered by a horny material.
examples: The bird carried a seed in its beak.
The eagle has a strong, hooked beak.
The duck dipped its beak into the water.

senses.definition: A projecting mouthpart or similar structure in certain animals, especially when resembling a bird's beak.
examples: The turtle has a sharp beak instead of teeth.
The squid uses its hard beak to tear food.
The octopus has a powerful beak at the center of its arms.

senses.definition: A pointed or projecting part of an object that resembles the beak of a bird.
examples: The vessel had a beak-shaped projection at its front.
The tool ended in a narrow metal beak.
The helmet featured a decorative beak above the face opening.

beam.etymology: From Old English beam, meaning tree, piece of timber, or wooden structure; later extended to structural supports and rays of light
beam.explanation: Refers to a long, strong piece of material used to support a structure, or to a narrow stream of light, energy, or radiation. As a verb, beam can mean to shine brightly, transmit something electronically, or smile broadly with happiness or pride.

senses.definition: Noun: a long, strong piece of wood, metal, concrete, or another material used to support a building or structure.
examples: The roof is supported by several wooden beams.
Workers lifted the steel beam into position.
The old house had exposed beams across the ceiling.

senses.definition: Noun: a narrow stream or ray of light, energy, or radiation.
examples: A beam of sunlight entered through the window.
The flashlight produced a narrow beam.
Scientists directed a laser beam at the target.

senses.definition: Noun: a long horizontal structural member used in certain machines, vehicles, or pieces of equipment.
examples: The gymnast balanced carefully on the beam.
The machine has a reinforced cross beam.
The load was suspended from an overhead beam.

senses.definition: Noun: the width of a ship or boat at its widest point.
examples: The vessel has a beam of nearly twenty feet.
A wider beam can provide greater stability.
The designers increased the ship's beam.

senses.definition: Verb: to shine or send out light.
examples: Sunlight beamed through the clouds.
The headlights beamed across the dark road.
A spotlight beamed onto the stage.

senses.definition: Verb: to smile broadly because of happiness, pride, or satisfaction.
examples: She beamed with pride at her son's achievement.
He beamed when he heard the good news.
The children beamed at the audience after the performance.

senses.definition: Verb: to transmit a signal, image, program, or information electronically from one place to another.
examples: The satellite beamed the signal back to Earth.
The ceremony was beamed around the world.
Images were beamed directly to the control center.

bean.etymology: From Old English bean, referring to the seed or plant of various legumes
bean.explanation: Refers primarily to an edible seed produced by certain plants in the legume family. The word can also refer to the plant that produces such seeds or, more broadly, to certain seeds that resemble beans, such as coffee beans.

senses.definition: An edible seed produced by certain plants of the legume family.
examples: She added beans to the soup.
The meal included rice and black beans.
He soaked the dried beans overnight before cooking them.

senses.definition: A plant that produces edible beans, usually in pods.
examples: The bean plants grew quickly in the garden.
She planted several rows of beans in the spring.
The bean climbed the support as it grew.

senses.definition: A seed or seedlike object resembling a bean, especially one used to produce food or beverages.
examples: The coffee beans were roasted that morning.
She ground the beans before making coffee.
Cocoa beans are processed to make chocolate.

senses.definition: A small object or shape resembling a bean.
examples: The toy contained several colorful bean-shaped pieces.
The cushion was filled with tiny plastic beans.
The design featured a curved bean shape.

bear.etymology: The noun meaning the animal comes from Old English bera. The verb comes from Old English beran, meaning to carry, support, bring forth, or endure. Although spelled and pronounced alike today, these major senses developed from separate Old English words.
bear.explanation: As a noun, bear refers primarily to a large, heavily built mammal with thick fur and strong limbs. As a verb, it has several common meanings, including to carry or support something, endure something difficult, accept responsibility, produce offspring or fruit, and move or turn in a particular direction.

senses.definition: Noun: a large, powerful mammal with thick fur, a short tail, and strong limbs, belonging to the family Ursidae.
examples: A bear emerged from the forest.
The hikers saw a black bear near the trail.
Bears spend much of their time searching for food.

senses.definition: Noun: in finance, a person who expects the price of a security, market, or other asset to decline.
examples: The bears expected stock prices to fall further.
He became a bear after reviewing the company's weak earnings.
Bulls and bears disagreed about the market's direction.

senses.definition: Verb: to carry, hold, or support the weight of someone or something.
examples: The bridge must bear the weight of heavy trucks.
She bore the box carefully across the room.
The columns bear the weight of the roof.

senses.definition: Verb: to endure, tolerate, or withstand something difficult, painful, or unpleasant.
examples: She could barely bear the pain.
He could not bear the thought of losing his home.
The equipment was designed to bear extreme temperatures.

senses.definition: Verb: to accept, possess, or carry responsibility, blame, a cost, or another obligation.
examples: The company must bear the cost of the repairs.
She bears responsibility for managing the project.
Both sides bear some blame for the failure.

senses.definition: Verb: to have, display, or carry a particular feature, mark, name, or resemblance.
examples: The document bears his signature.
The child bears a strong resemblance to her mother.
The building bears the name of its founder.

senses.definition: Verb: to give birth to offspring or produce fruit, flowers, or another natural product.
examples: The tree bears fruit every summer.
The mare bore a healthy foal.
These plants begin to bear flowers in early spring.

senses.definition: Verb: to move, turn, or proceed in a particular direction.
examples: Bear left at the next intersection.
The trail bears north after crossing the river.
The ship bore toward the coast.

beard.etymology: From Old English beard, meaning the hair growing on the chin and lower part of the face
beard.explanation: Refers primarily to the hair that grows on the chin, cheeks, and lower part of a man's face. The word can also describe similar hairlike or bristly growths on animals or plants. As a verb, beard can mean to confront someone boldly or directly.

senses.definition: Noun: hair that grows on the chin, cheeks, and lower part of a person's face, especially an adult man's face.
examples: He grew a beard during the winter.
The barber trimmed his beard.
His beard had begun to turn gray.

senses.definition: Noun: a growth of hair, bristles, feathers, or similar material on an animal or plant that resembles a human beard.
examples: The goat had a long beard beneath its chin.
The bird has a small tuft resembling a beard.
The grain develops a beard of stiff bristles.

senses.definition: Verb: to confront, challenge, or oppose someone boldly, especially someone powerful or intimidating.
examples: She bearded the powerful official in his own office.
Few people were willing to beard the director over the decision.
The reformer became known for bearding influential opponents.

bearer.etymology: Formed from bear, in the sense of carrying, holding, or conveying something, with the agent suffix -er
bearer.explanation: Refers to a person or thing that carries, holds, presents, or conveys something. The word is commonly used for someone carrying an object, message, document, title, or responsibility, and can also describe a person or organism carrying a disease or other biological agent.

senses.definition: A person who carries or transports something.
examples: The bearer carried the ceremonial flag into the hall.
Several bearers lifted the heavy object.
The torch bearer entered the stadium.

senses.definition: A person who brings, delivers, or communicates something, especially a message or news.
examples: She was the bearer of good news.
The messenger became the bearer of an important warning.
He disliked being the bearer of bad news.

senses.definition: A person who possesses, holds, or presents a document, title, right, or other item.
examples: The ticket admits the bearer to the event.
The certificate entitles the bearer to claim the prize.
The document must be presented by its lawful bearer.

senses.definition: A person who holds or carries a particular title, office, responsibility, quality, or characteristic.
examples: The office bearer represented the organization at the meeting.
She became the bearer of an important family tradition.
The title bearer served in the position for many years.

senses.definition: A person, animal, or organism that carries and may transmit a disease, infection, gene, or other biological agent.
examples: The mosquito can act as a bearer of disease.
A person may be a bearer of the infection without showing symptoms.
Researchers identified the animal as a possible bearer of the pathogen.

senses.definition: In finance, the holder of a negotiable financial instrument whose ownership is determined by physical possession rather than by registration.
examples: The bond was payable to the bearer.
Bearer securities can be transferred by delivering the document.
The issuer made payment to whoever was the lawful bearer of the certificate.

beast.etymology: From Middle English beste, from Old French beste, ultimately from Latin bestia, meaning animal or wild creature
beast.explanation: Refers primarily to an animal, especially a large, wild, or dangerous one. It can also be used figuratively for a cruel or violent person, something extremely difficult or powerful, or informally for a person who is exceptionally strong or capable.

senses.definition: An animal, especially a large, wild, or dangerous one.
examples: The hunters tracked the beast through the forest.
Legends told of a strange beast living in the mountains.
The wounded beast disappeared into the trees.

senses.definition: A cruel, violent, or uncivilized person.
examples: The villain was portrayed as a heartless beast.
He behaved like a beast toward the prisoners.
She condemned the attacker as a brutal beast.

senses.definition: Something unusually large, powerful, difficult, or demanding.
examples: The old truck is a beast to drive.
That examination was an absolute beast.
The new computer is a beast when it comes to processing large datasets.

senses.definition: Informal: a person who is exceptionally strong, skilled, energetic, or effective.
examples: She is a beast on the basketball court.
He trained like a beast throughout the summer.
Their new defensive player is an absolute beast.

beat.etymology: From Old English beatan, meaning to strike, pound, or hit repeatedly
beat.explanation: As a verb, beat can mean to strike repeatedly, defeat an opponent, move rhythmically, or perform better than something else. As a noun, it can refer to a repeated rhythm, a single pulse or stroke, or a regular area assigned to someone such as a police officer. Informally, beat can also mean extremely tired.
usageNotes: The past tense of beat is also beat. The past participle is usually beaten, as in 'They have beaten the record.'

senses.definition: Verb: to strike someone or something repeatedly.
examples: Rain beat against the windows.
He beat the rug to remove the dust.
The drummer beat the drum with two sticks.

senses.definition: Verb: to defeat a person or team in a competition, game, or contest.
examples: Our team beat its rival in the final game.
She beat the defending champion in three sets.
They believed they could beat any team in the league.

senses.definition: Verb: to perform better than, exceed, or surpass a result, record, price, or standard.
examples: She beat the previous record by two seconds.
The new system beat expectations.
No competitor could beat their price.

senses.definition: Verb: to mix or stir ingredients rapidly and repeatedly.
examples: Beat the eggs until they become smooth.
She beat the cream with an electric mixer.
He beat the batter until all the lumps disappeared.

senses.definition: Verb: to move or pulse in a regular rhythm, especially of the heart.
examples: His heart began to beat faster.
The bird's wings beat rapidly.
She could hear the clock beating steadily in the quiet room.

senses.definition: Noun: a regular repeated rhythm, pulse, or movement, especially in music.
examples: The song has a strong beat.
She tapped her foot to the beat.
The drummer kept a steady beat throughout the performance.

senses.definition: Noun: a single stroke, pulse, or rhythmic movement.
examples: His heart skipped a beat.
The conductor counted four beats to each measure.
There was a brief pause between each beat.

senses.definition: Noun: a regular route, area, or subject assigned to someone as part of a job, especially a police officer or journalist.
examples: The officer walked his usual beat downtown.
She covers the education beat for the newspaper.
The reporter spent several years on the political beat.

senses.definition: Adjective, informal: extremely tired or exhausted.
examples: I'm beat after working all day.
They were completely beat after the long hike.
She went straight to bed because she was beat.

beautiful.etymology: Formed from beauty with the adjective-forming suffix -ful, meaning full of beauty or possessing qualities that give pleasure to the senses or mind
beautiful.explanation: Describes someone or something that is highly attractive, pleasing, admirable, or delightful. It can refer to physical appearance, natural scenery, artistic works, ideas, experiences, or anything regarded as especially pleasing or excellent.

senses.definition: Very attractive or pleasing to look at.
examples: The garden was filled with beautiful flowers.
She wore a beautiful blue dress.
They admired the beautiful mountain scenery.

senses.definition: Pleasing to the senses, emotions, or mind.
examples: The orchestra performed a beautiful piece of music.
She has a beautiful singing voice.
The poem expresses a beautiful idea about friendship.

senses.definition: Having admirable, graceful, or excellent qualities.
examples: It was a beautiful act of kindness.
The two dancers performed with beautiful precision.
The architect created a beautiful solution to a difficult design problem.

senses.definition: Informal: exceptionally good, successful, or satisfying.
examples: He made a beautiful pass to set up the winning goal.
The mechanic did a beautiful job repairing the car.
Everything worked out beautifully after a difficult start.

beautifully.etymology: Formed from beautiful with the adverb-forming suffix -ly, meaning in a beautiful, pleasing, graceful, or excellent manner
beautifully.explanation: Describes something done in an attractive, graceful, pleasing, or highly effective manner. It can refer to physical appearance, artistic performance, behavior, craftsmanship, or the successful execution of an action.

senses.definition: In a way that is very attractive or pleasing to the senses.
examples: The room was beautifully decorated.
The flowers bloomed beautifully in the garden.
The sunset beautifully illuminated the mountains.

senses.definition: In a graceful, skillful, or artistic manner.
examples: She sang beautifully during the concert.
The dancers moved beautifully across the stage.
The musician played the difficult passage beautifully.

senses.definition: In an excellent, successful, or highly effective manner.
examples: The plan worked beautifully.
The new software performed beautifully during the demonstration.
The two materials blend beautifully together.

beauty.etymology: From Middle English beaute, from Old French beauté, ultimately from Latin bellus, meaning beautiful, fine, or pleasant
beauty.explanation: Refers to the quality of being physically, emotionally, or aesthetically pleasing. It can also describe an attractive person or thing, an especially admirable feature, or the pleasing qualities found in art, nature, ideas, or experiences.

senses.definition: The quality of being attractive, pleasing, or satisfying to the senses or mind.
examples: They admired the beauty of the landscape.
The painting is known for its simplicity and beauty.
She appreciated the beauty of the old building.

senses.definition: An attractive or pleasing person, object, place, or other thing.
examples: That antique car is a real beauty.
The garden was filled with natural beauties.
The restored house is an absolute beauty.

senses.definition: A particularly admirable, useful, or pleasing feature or advantage of something.
examples: The beauty of the system is its simplicity.
The beauty of the plan is that it requires very little equipment.
One beauty of the design is that it can be easily modified.

senses.definition: The study, practice, or business of improving personal appearance, especially through cosmetics, hair care, and skin care.
examples: She works in the beauty industry.
The store has a large beauty department.
He enrolled in a beauty school to study cosmetology.

beaver.etymology: From Old English beofor, referring to the large semiaquatic rodent known for building dams and lodges
beaver.explanation: Refers primarily to a large semiaquatic rodent with a broad, flat tail and strong teeth, known for cutting trees and building dams and lodges. As a verb, usually in the expression 'beaver away,' it means to work steadily and energetically.

senses.definition: A large semiaquatic rodent with a broad, flat tail and strong front teeth, known for cutting trees and building dams and lodges.
examples: A beaver was swimming across the pond.
The beaver used branches to strengthen its dam.
Beavers can significantly change the landscape around streams and rivers.

senses.definition: The fur or pelt of a beaver, historically used for making clothing and hats.
examples: Beaver fur was once highly valued in the hat-making industry.
Traders exchanged beaver pelts for manufactured goods.
The demand for beaver helped drive the North American fur trade.

senses.definition: Verb, usually in the phrase 'beaver away': to work steadily, busily, and persistently at a task.
examples: She beavered away at the report all afternoon.
The students were beavering away on their projects.
He continued to beaver away until the repairs were finished.

because.etymology: From Middle English because, originally formed from by cause, meaning by reason or on account of
because.explanation: Introduces the reason, cause, or explanation for something. It connects an event, statement, or situation with the reason that explains why it happened or is true.

senses.definition: For the reason that; used to introduce the cause or explanation of an action, event, or situation.
examples: We stayed indoors because it was raining.
She smiled because she was happy.
The game was canceled because the field was flooded.

senses.definition: Used to introduce the reason supporting a statement, decision, belief, or conclusion.
examples: I believe him because his explanation matches the evidence.
They chose the smaller building because it was less expensive.
The committee rejected the proposal because it lacked sufficient detail.

become.etymology: From Old English becuman, meaning to come to, arrive, happen, or come into a particular condition, formed from be- and cuman, meaning to come
become.explanation: Means to begin to be something, develop into a particular condition, or acquire a new quality or status. In a less common sense, become can also mean to suit someone or make that person appear attractive or appropriate.

senses.definition: To begin to be or develop into a particular state, condition, quality, or type of person or thing.
examples: The weather became colder during the evening.
She hopes to become a doctor.
The small company eventually became a major corporation.

senses.definition: To acquire a particular role, position, status, or identity.
examples: He became president of the organization.
The town became an important center of trade.
She became the first person in her family to graduate from college.

senses.definition: To gradually develop or change in a particular way.
examples: The problem became more serious over time.
The child became increasingly confident.
The two communities became closely connected.

senses.definition: To suit or look attractive or appropriate on someone.
