Figuratively, it means a detailed plan, model, or set of instructions for achieving a goal or creating something. As a verb, blueprint means to plan or design something in detail.

senses.definition: Noun: a detailed technical drawing or plan showing how a building, machine, system, or other structure is to be constructed.
examples: The architect reviewed the building's blueprint.
Workers followed the blueprints during construction.
The engineer prepared a detailed blueprint for the new machine.

senses.definition: Noun: a detailed plan, model, or set of instructions for achieving a particular goal.
examples: The report provides a blueprint for economic reform.
Their strategy became a blueprint for future projects.
The organization developed a blueprint for expanding its services.

senses.definition: Noun: a basic pattern, model, or structure from which something develops.
examples: DNA contains the biological blueprint for many inherited characteristics.
The constitution served as a blueprint for the new government.
The early design became the blueprint for later versions.

senses.definition: Verb: to plan, design, or outline something in detail before it is created or carried out.
examples: The committee blueprinted the expansion several years in advance.
Engineers blueprinted the new production system.
The organization carefully blueprinted its long-term strategy.

bluff.etymology: The word has several historical sources. Bluff meaning a steep cliff probably developed from a Dutch or related Germanic word meaning broad or flat. Bluff meaning to deceive arose later, especially from card-playing, where a player pretends to have a stronger hand than is actually held.
bluff.explanation: As a noun, bluff can mean an attempt to deceive someone by pretending to be stronger, more confident, or better prepared than one really is, or it can mean a steep cliff or high bank. As a verb, bluff means to deceive or intimidate through confident pretense. As an adjective, bluff can describe someone who is direct, hearty, and straightforward in manner.
usageNotes: In card games such as poker, bluff commonly refers to pretending to have a stronger hand than one actually has.
The expression 'call someone's bluff' means to challenge a person's threat or claim in order to discover whether it is genuine.

senses.definition: Noun: an attempt to deceive or intimidate someone by pretending to have greater strength, confidence, knowledge, or resources than one actually has.
examples: His threat turned out to be a bluff.
The negotiators suspected that the deadline was only a bluff.
She called his bluff and refused to change her position.

senses.definition: Noun: in a card game, an attempt to make other players believe that one's hand is stronger than it really is.
examples: He won the pot with a successful bluff.
The other players did not recognize her bluff.
A good bluff can force an opponent to fold.

senses.definition: Verb: to deceive or intimidate someone by pretending to possess greater strength, confidence, knowledge, or advantage than is actually the case.
examples: He tried to bluff his way past the guard.
The company attempted to bluff its competitors.
She bluffed the other players into folding.

senses.definition: Noun: a steep cliff, bank, or high area of land, especially one overlooking water or lower ground.
examples: They stood on a bluff overlooking the river.
The house was built near the top of a coastal bluff.
Trees covered the steep bluff above the beach.

senses.definition: Adjective: direct, hearty, and straightforward in manner, sometimes in a rough or abrupt way.
examples: He had a bluff but friendly manner.
The captain was known for his bluff honesty.
Her bluff style could seem abrupt to strangers.

blunt.etymology: From Middle English blunt, meaning dull, obtuse, or lacking a sharp edge or point; its earlier origin is uncertain
blunt.explanation: Describes something that is not sharp or pointed. It can also describe speech or behavior that is very direct and sometimes lacking in tact. As a verb, blunt means to make something less sharp, intense, effective, or sensitive. As a noun, blunt can informally refer to a cigar whose tobacco has been replaced partly or entirely with cannabis.

senses.definition: Adjective: having an edge or point that is not sharp.
examples: The knife had become too blunt to cut the rope.
He used the blunt end of the tool.
The pencil was blunt and needed sharpening.

senses.definition: Adjective: expressed in a very direct, frank, or straightforward manner, sometimes without sensitivity or tact.
examples: She gave him a blunt answer.
The manager was blunt about the company's financial problems.
His blunt criticism surprised the rest of the group.

senses.definition: Adjective: having a broad, rounded, or nonpointed shape.
examples: The animal has a short, blunt snout.
The tool has a blunt tip for safety.
The leaves end in blunt points.

senses.definition: Verb: to make an edge or point less sharp.
examples: Repeated use blunted the blade.
Striking the stone had blunted the tool.
The hard material quickly blunted the cutting edge.

senses.definition: Verb: to reduce the strength, intensity, effectiveness, or emotional impact of something.
examples: The medication helped blunt the pain.
Higher costs blunted the effect of the tax reduction.
The defensive measures blunted the attack.

senses.definition: Verb: to make a person's feelings, awareness, or sensitivity less acute.
examples: Years of routine had blunted his enthusiasm.
Exhaustion blunted her concentration.
Repeated exposure can blunt a person's reaction to the warning.

senses.definition: Noun, informal: a cigar that has been emptied and refilled partly or entirely with cannabis.
examples: The term blunt is used informally for a particular form of cannabis cigar.
The report referred to the object as a blunt.
The word blunt has a specialized slang meaning in addition to its ordinary uses.

blur.etymology: Probably from a Germanic source and related to words describing stains, smears, or indistinct marks; its precise origin is uncertain
blur.explanation: As a noun, blur refers to something that appears unclear, indistinct, or out of focus. As a verb, it means to make something difficult to see, distinguish, remember, or understand clearly. It can refer to physical vision and images as well as figurative distinctions, memories, or boundaries.
usageNotes: The final consonant is doubled before endings beginning with a vowel: blur becomes blurred and blurring.

senses.definition: Noun: an indistinct or unclear shape, image, or appearance.
examples: The speeding car passed in a blur.
Without her glasses, everything looked like a blur.
The photograph showed only a blur of movement.

senses.definition: Noun: something remembered or experienced without clear detail.
examples: The hectic week passed in a blur.
Much of the evening was a blur in his memory.
The events following the accident became a blur.

senses.definition: Verb: to make an image, object, or view unclear or out of focus.
examples: Rain blurred the view through the window.
Movement blurred the photograph.
Tears blurred her vision.

senses.definition: Verb: to become visually unclear or indistinct.
examples: The words began to blur as his eyes grew tired.
The distant buildings blurred in the fog.
The image blurred when the camera moved.

senses.definition: Verb: to make a distinction, boundary, memory, or idea less clear or definite.
examples: Technology has blurred the boundary between work and home.
The passage of time blurred some of his memories.
The new arrangement blurred the distinction between the two roles.

board.etymology: From Old English bord, meaning a plank, flat surface, table, or side of a ship, from a Germanic source
board.explanation: Refers to a flat piece of wood or other material, a surface used for writing or displaying information, or a group of people responsible for directing an organization. It can also mean meals and lodging. As a verb, board means to enter a ship, airplane, train, or other vehicle, to provide meals and lodging, or to cover something with boards.

senses.definition: Noun: a long, flat, relatively thin piece of wood or another rigid material.
examples: He cut the board to the correct length.
The workers placed several boards across the opening.
She painted the wooden board white.

senses.definition: Noun: a flat surface used for writing, displaying information, playing a game, or performing another activity.
examples: The teacher wrote the answer on the board.
The schedule was posted on the notice board.
They arranged the chess pieces on the board.

senses.definition: Noun: a group of people appointed or elected to manage, supervise, advise, or govern an organization.
examples: The board approved the annual budget.
She serves on the university's board of trustees.
The company's board met to discuss the merger.

senses.definition: Noun: regular meals provided as part of an arrangement for lodging or residence.
examples: The cost includes room and board.
He worked at the farm in exchange for board.
Students pay separately for tuition and board.

senses.definition: Verb: to enter or get onto a ship, aircraft, train, bus, or other form of transportation.
examples: Passengers began to board the airplane.
We boarded the train just before departure.
The crew boarded the ship early in the morning.

senses.definition: Verb: to live somewhere and receive meals, especially in exchange for payment.
examples: She boarded with a family near the university.
Several students board at the school during the term.
He boarded with relatives while looking for an apartment.

senses.definition: Verb: to provide someone or an animal with lodging and meals or care.
examples: The school boards students from distant communities.
They boarded their dog at a kennel during the trip.
The family agreed to board two visiting students.

senses.definition: Verb: to cover, close, or secure something with wooden boards or similar panels.
examples: Workers boarded the windows before the storm.
The abandoned building was boarded up.
They boarded over the damaged doorway.

boast.etymology: From Middle English bosten, meaning to brag or speak proudly, probably from an Anglo-French or Germanic source; its earlier origin is uncertain
boast.explanation: As a verb, boast means to speak with excessive pride about one's achievements, possessions, abilities, or qualities. It can also mean to possess or feature something impressive. As a noun, a boast is a proud or self-important statement about something a person has done or possesses.

senses.definition: Verb: to speak with excessive pride about one's achievements, abilities, possessions, or qualities.
examples: He boasted about winning the competition.
She rarely boasts about her accomplishments.
The athlete boasted that no one could defeat him.

senses.definition: Verb: to possess, contain, or feature something considered impressive or desirable.
examples: The city boasts several excellent museums.
The hotel boasts a large swimming pool.
The university boasts one of the region's largest libraries.

senses.definition: Noun: a proud, confident, or self-important statement about an achievement, possession, or ability.
examples: His claim sounded more like a boast than a fact.
She made no boast about her success.
The team's boast of an undefeated season ended after its first loss.

senses.definition: Noun: something regarded as a source of particular pride.
examples: The historic theater is one of the town's greatest boasts.
The university's research center is a major boast of the institution.
The region's natural beauty is one of its proudest boasts.

boat.etymology: From Old English bat, meaning a boat or vessel, from a Germanic source
boat.explanation: Refers to a relatively small vessel designed to travel on water. Boats may be powered by oars, sails, engines, or other means and are used for transportation, fishing, recreation, rescue, and many other purposes. As a verb, boat means to travel, transport, or engage in recreation by boat.

senses.definition: Noun: a relatively small vessel used for traveling on water.
examples: They crossed the lake in a small boat.
The boat returned to the harbor before sunset.
Several boats were tied to the dock.

senses.definition: Noun: a watercraft designed for a particular activity, such as fishing, sailing, recreation, transportation, or rescue.
examples: The fishermen left shore in their boat before dawn.
The rescue boat reached the stranded passengers.
They rented a sailboat for the afternoon.

senses.definition: Verb: to travel or move on water in a boat.
examples: They boated across the lake.
We spent the afternoon boating along the coast.
The family boats on the river during the summer.

senses.definition: Verb: to carry or transport someone or something by boat.
examples: Supplies were boated across the river.
The workers boated the equipment to the island.
Visitors were boated from the dock to the ship.

body.etymology: From Old English bodig, meaning the physical form of a person or animal
body.explanation: Refers primarily to the physical structure of a person or animal. It can also mean the main part of an object, a large amount or mass of something, an organized group of people, or a collection of information or knowledge. As a verb, body can mean to give physical form to something or, in certain technical contexts, to form the main structure of an object.

senses.definition: Noun: the physical structure of a person or animal.
examples: Regular exercise helps keep the body healthy.
The human body contains many complex systems.
The animal used its entire body to push through the opening.

senses.definition: Noun: the main or central part of a person, animal, object, or structure, excluding attached or projecting parts.
examples: The insect has a long narrow body.
The body of the airplane was damaged during the storm.
The guitar has a wooden body.

senses.definition: Noun: the dead physical remains of a person or animal.
examples: The body was recovered from the wreckage.
Investigators examined the body for evidence.
The animal's body was removed from the roadway.

senses.definition: Noun: an organized group of people having a particular purpose, authority, or function.
examples: The governing body approved the proposal.
The university has a large student body.
The legislative body met for a special session.

senses.definition: Noun: a large quantity, mass, or area of a particular substance.
examples: The lake is a large body of fresh water.
Astronomers observed a distant celestial body.
A body of warm air moved across the region.

senses.definition: Noun: a substantial collection of facts, ideas, literature, evidence, or knowledge.
examples: Researchers have developed a large body of evidence.
The course introduces students to the body of literature on the subject.
A growing body of research supports the conclusion.

senses.definition: Noun: the main portion of a written work, speech, document, or message, excluding introductory or supplementary material.
examples: The body of the report contains the detailed findings.
She explained the argument in the body of the essay.
The main evidence appears in the body of the article.

senses.definition: Noun: fullness, thickness, strength, or substantial quality in a substance such as hair, fabric, food, or a beverage.
examples: The conditioner gives her hair more body.
The wine has a rich, full body.
The fabric has enough body to hold its shape.

senses.definition: Verb: to give physical form, substance, or shape to something.
examples: The sculptor bodied the figure in clay.
The design was bodied forth in a detailed model.
The artist gradually bodied the character into a recognizable form.

boil.etymology: From Old French boillir, meaning to boil or bubble, from Latin bullire, meaning to bubble or seethe
boil.explanation: As a verb, boil means to heat a liquid until it reaches the temperature at which it forms bubbles and turns into vapor, or to cook food in such a liquid. It can also describe intense anger or turbulent movement. As a noun, a boil can mean the state or process of boiling or a painful, pus-filled swelling of the skin.

senses.definition: Verb: to heat a liquid until it reaches a temperature at which bubbles form throughout it and it begins changing into vapor.
examples: Boil the water before adding the pasta.
The water began to boil rapidly.
She boiled a pot of water for tea.

senses.definition: Verb: to cook food in boiling water or another hot liquid.
examples: She boiled the potatoes until they were tender.
Boil the eggs for several minutes.
They boiled the vegetables in lightly salted water.

senses.definition: Verb: for a liquid to bubble, churn, or move violently.
examples: The soup boiled over onto the stove.
The river seemed to boil around the rocks.
Steam rose as the mixture boiled.

senses.definition: Verb, figurative: to feel or express intense anger or agitation.
examples: He was boiling with anger after hearing the accusation.
She could feel her frustration beginning to boil.
Tensions boiled beneath the surface throughout the meeting.

senses.definition: Noun: the state or process of boiling.
examples: Bring the water to a boil.
Reduce the heat once the soup reaches a boil.
The mixture came to a rapid boil.

senses.definition: Noun: a painful, swollen skin infection containing pus, usually caused by infection of a hair follicle or surrounding tissue.
examples: A painful boil developed on his arm.
The doctor examined the boil for signs of infection.
She kept the area around the boil clean.

bold.etymology: From Old English beald, meaning brave, confident, or courageous, from a Germanic source
bold.explanation: Describes someone who is brave, confident, or willing to take risks. It can also describe an action, idea, design, color, or statement that is striking, noticeable, or strongly expressed. In printing and digital text, bold refers to a heavier and darker style of type used for emphasis.

senses.definition: Adjective: brave, confident, and willing to take risks or face danger.
examples: She made a bold decision to start her own company.
The explorers attempted a bold journey across the mountains.
His bold actions impressed the rest of the team.

senses.definition: Adjective: direct, confident, or forceful in manner or expression.
examples: He made a bold claim during the debate.
She approached the problem with a bold attitude.
The proposal offered a bold vision for the future.

senses.definition: Adjective: striking, vivid, or highly noticeable in appearance.
examples: The room was decorated with bold colors.
She chose a dress with a bold pattern.
The building has a bold modern design.

senses.definition: Adjective: printed or displayed in thick, dark characters for emphasis.
examples: The heading appears in bold type.
Important terms are printed in bold letters.
Make the title bold so that it stands out.

senses.definition: Noun: a bold style of type or text used for emphasis.
examples: Use bold for the main headings.
The editor changed the important terms to bold.
Too much bold can make a page difficult to scan.

bolt.etymology: From Old English bolt, meaning a short, heavy arrow or projectile. The word later developed meanings for similarly shaped metal fasteners, locking devices, flashes of lightning, and sudden rapid movement.
bolt.explanation: Refers to a metal fastener, a sliding locking device, a flash of lightning, or a long roll of fabric. As a verb, bolt can mean to fasten something, to run away suddenly, or for an animal to move unexpectedly and rapidly.

senses.definition: Noun: a metal fastener, usually consisting of a threaded shaft used with a nut to hold objects together.
examples: The mechanic tightened the bolt with a wrench.
A loose bolt caused the machine to vibrate.
Workers used steel bolts to secure the frame.

senses.definition: Noun: a sliding metal bar used to lock or secure a door, gate, or similar structure.
examples: She pushed the bolt into place before going to bed.
The gate was secured with a heavy iron bolt.
He drew back the bolt and opened the door.

senses.definition: Noun: a bright flash of lightning.
examples: A bolt of lightning struck the tree.
Several lightning bolts flashed across the sky.
A sudden bolt illuminated the entire valley.

senses.definition: Noun: a long roll or measured length of fabric.
examples: She purchased a bolt of blue fabric.
The shop displayed several bolts of silk.
He carried the heavy bolt of cloth to the cutting table.

senses.definition: Noun: a short, heavy projectile traditionally fired from a crossbow.
examples: The crossbow fired a heavy bolt.
Several bolts were stored beside the weapon.
The bolt struck the wooden target.

senses.definition: Verb: to fasten or secure something with a bolt or bolts.
examples: He bolted the door before leaving the room.
The frame was bolted to the floor.
Workers bolted the sections together.

senses.definition: Verb: to run or move away suddenly and rapidly.
examples: The frightened horse bolted from the stable.
The dog bolted through the open gate.
He bolted from the room when he heard the alarm.

senses.definition: Verb: to suddenly abandon, leave, or withdraw from a group, agreement, or situation.
examples: Several members bolted from the organization.
The investor bolted when the negotiations collapsed.
Two representatives bolted from the coalition.

senses.definition: Verb: to swallow food very quickly.
examples: He bolted his breakfast and rushed out the door.
She bolted down the sandwich between meetings.
The hungry child bolted the meal in a few minutes.

bomb.etymology: From French bombe and Italian bomba, ultimately from Latin bombus and Greek bombos, meaning a booming or humming sound
bomb.explanation: Refers primarily to an explosive device designed to release destructive force when detonated. As a verb, bomb means to attack or damage a place with bombs. Informally, it can also mean to fail badly, while the expression 'the bomb' can mean something considered excellent or impressive.

senses.definition: Noun: an explosive device designed to release destructive force when detonated.
examples: Police discovered a bomb in the abandoned building.
The area was evacuated after reports of a possible bomb.
The explosion was caused by a concealed bomb.

senses.definition: Noun: a weapon containing explosive material that is dropped, launched, placed, or otherwise delivered toward a target.
examples: The aircraft carried several bombs.
The unexploded bomb was discovered decades after the war.
Residents took shelter during the bomb attack.

senses.definition: Verb: to attack, strike, or damage a place or target with bombs.
examples: Aircraft bombed the military installation.
The city was heavily bombed during the war.
The attackers threatened to bomb the facility.

senses.definition: Verb, informal: to perform or fail very badly.
examples: The movie bombed at the box office.
He worried that he would bomb the interview.
The new product bombed despite an expensive advertising campaign.

senses.definition: Noun, informal: a complete failure or something that performs very poorly.
examples: The film was a box-office bomb.
The expensive product turned out to be a bomb.
Critics called the show a commercial bomb.

senses.definition: Noun, informal: something considered exceptionally good, impressive, or enjoyable, especially in the expression 'the bomb.'
examples: That restaurant is the bomb.
Her new song is the bomb.
Everyone said the party was the bomb.

bombard.etymology: From French bombarder, meaning to attack with artillery, from bombarde, an early type of cannon or large gun
bombard.explanation: Means to attack a place or target repeatedly with artillery, bombs, or other projectiles. Figuratively, it means to overwhelm someone or something with a large amount of questions, information, criticism, requests, or other repeated activity. In science, bombard can also mean to direct particles or radiation at a material or target.

senses.definition: To attack a place or target repeatedly with artillery, bombs, missiles, or other projectiles.
examples: The forces bombarded the defensive positions.
The city was bombarded for several days.
Artillery units bombarded the target from a distance.

senses.definition: To overwhelm someone with a large number of questions, messages, requests, criticisms, or other things in a short period.
examples: Reporters bombarded the official with questions.
The company was bombarded with customer complaints.
She was bombarded with emails after the announcement.

senses.definition: To expose or strike a substance or target repeatedly with particles, radiation, or other forms of energy.
examples: Scientists bombarded the material with electrons.
The researchers bombarded the atoms with high-energy particles.
The sample was bombarded with radiation during the experiment.

bomber.etymology: Formed from bomb with the agent or instrument suffix -er, referring to a person or aircraft that carries out bombing
bomber.explanation: Refers to a military aircraft designed to carry and release bombs or other explosive weapons. It can also refer to a person who carries out a bombing or uses an explosive device in an attack.

senses.definition: A military aircraft designed primarily to carry and release bombs or other explosive weapons against targets.
examples: The bomber returned to its airfield after the mission.
Several bombers were displayed at the aviation museum.
The aircraft was originally designed as a long-range bomber.

senses.definition: A person who carries out a bombing or uses an explosive device in an attack.
examples: Investigators worked to identify the bomber.
The suspected bomber was arrested after the attack.
Authorities searched for evidence connected to the bomber.

bombing.etymology: Formed from bomb with the noun-forming suffix -ing, referring to the act or process of attacking or damaging a target with bombs
bombing.explanation: Refers to an attack in which one or more explosive bombs are used against a person, place, structure, or other target. Bombing can be carried out from aircraft or by bombs placed, launched, or otherwise delivered to a target. The word can refer to a single attack or to repeated attacks during a military campaign or other conflict.
usageNotes: Bombing is also the present participle and gerund form of the verb bomb.

senses.definition: An attack in which one or more bombs are used against a target.
examples: The bombing damaged several buildings.
Authorities investigated the bombing immediately after the explosion.
Residents were evacuated following the bombing.

senses.definition: The military use of bombs against targets, especially from aircraft, often as part of a larger campaign.
examples: The bombing continued throughout the night.
Heavy bombing damaged transportation infrastructure.
The campaign included several weeks of aerial bombing.

senses.definition: The act of placing, delivering, or detonating an explosive bomb as part of an attack.
examples: Police arrested a suspect in connection with the bombing.
The memorial commemorates those killed in the bombing.
Investigators examined evidence from the site of the bombing.

bond.etymology: From Middle English bond or band, meaning a binding, restraint, or tie, from a Germanic source related to bind
bond.explanation: Refers to something that connects, joins, or holds people or things together. It can mean an emotional relationship, a chemical connection between atoms, an adhesive attachment, a financial security representing debt, or a legal guarantee involving money. As a verb, bond means to form a connection or attachment, either physically, chemically, financially, or emotionally.

senses.definition: Noun: a close emotional, social, or personal connection between people.
examples: The sisters share a strong bond.
Working together created a bond between the teammates.
Their friendship developed into a lasting bond.

senses.definition: Noun: something that connects, joins, or holds two or more things together.
examples: The adhesive formed a strong bond between the surfaces.
Trust can serve as a bond within a community.
The material creates a permanent bond with the metal.

senses.definition: Noun, chemistry: the force or connection that holds atoms or ions together in a molecule or compound.
examples: The molecule contains several chemical bonds.
A covalent bond forms when atoms share electrons.
Heat can weaken certain molecular bonds.

senses.definition: Noun, finance: a debt security in which an investor lends money to a government, company, or other issuer in return for repayment and usually interest.
examples: She invested part of her savings in government bonds.
The company issued bonds to finance the new project.
The bond pays interest twice each year.

senses.definition: Noun, law: money or another guarantee provided to secure a person's release from custody or ensure compliance with a legal obligation.
examples: The judge set bond at ten thousand dollars.
He was released after posting bond.
The court revoked her bond after she violated the conditions of release.

senses.definition: Verb: to form or develop a close personal or emotional relationship.
examples: The new employees bonded during the training program.
The child quickly bonded with the family.
They bonded over their shared interest in music.

senses.definition: Verb: to join, attach, or cause materials or substances to adhere to one another.
examples: The adhesive bonds the plastic to the metal.
The coating bonds firmly to the surface.
Heat was used to bond the two layers together.

senses.definition: Verb, chemistry: for atoms, ions, or molecules to form a chemical connection.
examples: The atoms bond by sharing electrons.
Hydrogen can bond with oxygen to form water.
The molecules bond strongly under these conditions.

bone.etymology: From Old English ban, meaning bone, from a Germanic source
bone.explanation: Refers primarily to the hard, living tissue that forms much of the skeleton of humans and other vertebrate animals. The word can also refer to an individual skeletal structure, material made from bone, or figuratively to the basic structure or essential part of something. As a verb, bone can mean to remove bones from food.

senses.definition: Noun: the hard living tissue that forms much of the skeleton of a vertebrate animal.
examples: Bone provides support and protection for the body.
The doctor examined the damaged bone.
Calcium is important for maintaining healthy bones.

senses.definition: Noun: one of the individual hard structures that make up a skeleton.
examples: He broke a bone in his hand.
The human body contains many different bones.
The dog buried a large bone in the yard.

senses.definition: Noun: bone material used to make tools, decorations, handles, or other objects.
examples: The artifact was carved from bone.
The handle was traditionally made of bone.
Archaeologists discovered several bone tools at the site.

senses.definition: Noun, figurative: the basic framework, structure, or essential part of something.
examples: The renovation preserved the bones of the original building.
The proposal has good bones but still needs more detail.
The basic bones of the system remained unchanged.

senses.definition: Verb: to remove the bones from meat, fish, or another food.
examples: She boned the chicken before cooking it.
The fish was carefully boned before serving.
The butcher boned the meat for the customer.

bonus.etymology: From Latin bonus, meaning good. In English, the word developed a financial sense referring to an extra payment or benefit given in addition to what is normally expected.
bonus.explanation: Refers to something extra that is given in addition to what is normally expected or required. It commonly means an additional payment made to an employee or other person as a reward or incentive, but it can also refer more generally to any added advantage, benefit, feature, or reward.

senses.definition: An additional payment given to an employee or other person beyond regular wages, salary, or compensation.
examples: Employees received a year-end bonus.
She earned a bonus for exceeding her sales target.
The company paid managers an annual performance bonus.

senses.definition: Something extra given as a reward, incentive, or benefit.
examples: The store offered a bonus with every qualifying purchase.
Customers received bonus points for using the service.
The package includes several bonus features.

senses.definition: An unexpected or additional advantage beyond what was originally expected.
examples: The larger office was an unexpected bonus.
Living close to work has the added bonus of reducing travel time.
The beautiful weather was a bonus during the vacation.

book.etymology: From Old English boc, meaning book, written document, or written work, from a Germanic source
book.explanation: Refers primarily to a written or printed work consisting of pages bound together or to its digital equivalent. A book may contain fiction, nonfiction, reference material, records, or other information. As a verb, book commonly means to reserve something in advance, arrange an engagement, or officially record a person or transaction.

senses.definition: Noun: a written or printed work consisting of pages bound together within a cover.
examples: She borrowed a book from the library.
He opened the book to the first chapter.
The shelf contains hundreds of books.

senses.definition: Noun: a written work published in printed or electronic form.
examples: She wrote a book about American history.
The book is available in both print and digital editions.
He downloaded the book to his tablet.

senses.definition: Noun: a set or collection of records, accounts, or other organized information.
examples: The accountant reviewed the company's books.
The transaction was entered in the books.
Investigators examined the financial books for irregularities.

senses.definition: Noun: one major division of a long written work.
examples: The poem is divided into twelve books.
The second book of the work introduces a new character.
Students read selections from several books of the ancient text.

senses.definition: Verb: to reserve or arrange something in advance, such as a room, seat, ticket, or appointment.
examples: We booked a hotel room for the weekend.
She booked an appointment with the dentist.
They booked their flights several months in advance.

senses.definition: Verb: to arrange for a performer, speaker, venue, or service to appear or be available at a particular time.
examples: The festival booked several local bands.
They booked the conference hall for Friday.
The agency booked her for three speaking engagements.

senses.definition: Verb: to officially record a person's name and alleged offense after an arrest.
examples: Police booked the suspect at the county jail.
He was arrested and booked on several charges.
The officer completed the paperwork after booking the defendant.

booking.etymology: Formed from book with the noun-forming suffix -ing, originally referring to the act of entering information into a book or record and later to making reservations, arranging engagements, and formally recording arrests
booking.explanation: Refers to an arrangement or reservation made in advance for travel, accommodations, entertainment, appointments, or services. It can also mean an engagement arranged for a performer or speaker, or the formal police process of recording information about an arrested person.
usageNotes: Booking is also the present participle and gerund form of the verb book.

senses.definition: An arrangement or reservation made in advance for a room, seat, ticket, trip, appointment, or service.
examples: She confirmed the hotel booking by email.
The restaurant requires a booking for large groups.
We made our flight booking several months in advance.

senses.definition: The act or process of reserving or arranging something in advance.
examples: Online booking is available through the company's website.
Early booking may provide lower prices.
The booking of conference rooms is handled by the office manager.

senses.definition: An arranged engagement for a performer, speaker, entertainer, or other professional.
examples: The singer received several new bookings for the summer.
Her agency arranged a television booking.
The comedian canceled a weekend booking because of illness.

senses.definition: The formal police process of recording identifying information, charges, and other details after a person has been arrested.
examples: The suspect was taken to the jail for booking.
Booking included fingerprinting and photographs.
He was released several hours after the booking process was completed.

booklet.etymology: Formed from book with the diminutive suffix -let, referring to a small book
booklet.explanation: Refers to a small, thin book with relatively few pages, often used to provide instructions, information, advertising, or educational material. Booklets may be stapled, folded, or otherwise simply bound.

senses.definition: A small, thin book containing a limited number of pages.
examples: The museum gave each visitor a small booklet.
She read the booklet while waiting for the program to begin.
The booklet contains twenty pages of illustrations and text.

senses.definition: A small publication containing instructions, information, explanations, or promotional material.
examples: The appliance came with an instruction booklet.
The school distributed a booklet explaining its programs.
The travel agency provided a booklet about local attractions.

bookmark.etymology: Formed from book and mark, originally referring to an object or mark used to identify a place in a book. The word later developed a computing sense for a saved link to a webpage or digital location.
bookmark.explanation: Refers to an object, strip, or other marker placed in a book to identify a particular page. In computing, a bookmark is a saved link or reference that allows a user to return quickly to a webpage, document location, or other digital resource. As a verb, bookmark means to mark or save something for later access.

senses.definition: Noun: an object or strip placed between the pages of a book to mark a place for later return.
examples: She placed a bookmark between the pages before closing the book.
The library gave each student a colorful bookmark.
He used a piece of paper as a bookmark.

senses.definition: Noun, computing: a saved link or reference that allows quick access to a webpage, file, document location, or other digital resource.
examples: She saved the website as a bookmark.
His browser contains hundreds of bookmarks.
I added the research page to my bookmarks.

senses.definition: Verb: to mark a page or location so that it can be easily found again.
examples: She bookmarked the chapter she wanted to review.
He bookmarked several important sections of the document.
The reading application allows users to bookmark individual pages.

senses.definition: Verb, computing: to save a link or digital location for quick access later.
examples: I bookmarked the article for future reference.
She bookmarked several useful websites.
You can bookmark the page instead of searching for it again.

bookshelf.etymology: Formed from book and shelf, referring to a shelf designed or used for storing books
bookshelf.explanation: Refers to a horizontal shelf used for storing, organizing, or displaying books. A bookshelf may be attached to a wall, built into furniture, or form part of a larger bookcase.
usageNotes: The plural of bookshelf is bookshelves, following the same spelling change as shelf to shelves.

senses.definition: A horizontal shelf used for holding, organizing, or displaying books.
examples: She placed the dictionary on the bookshelf.
The bookshelf was filled with history books.
He installed a new bookshelf above his desk.

senses.definition: A shelf forming part of a bookcase, cabinet, wall unit, or other piece of furniture intended for storing books.
examples: Each bookshelf in the cabinet can be adjusted.
The bottom bookshelf holds several large reference volumes.
They reinforced the bookshelf to support heavier books.

bookstore.etymology: Formed from book and store, referring to a retail business that sells books
bookstore.explanation: Refers to a retail shop or business that sells books. Bookstores may specialize in new books, used books, textbooks, rare books, or particular subjects, and many also sell magazines, stationery, gifts, or other related items.

senses.definition: A retail store that sells books.
examples: She bought the novel at a local bookstore.
The bookstore carries thousands of titles.
We stopped at the bookstore after lunch.

senses.definition: A business that specializes in selling a particular type or category of books.
examples: The university bookstore sells textbooks and academic materials.
They visited a used bookstore near the station.
The neighborhood has an independent bookstore specializing in history.

boom.etymology: Probably imitative in origin, representing a deep, resonant sound. Several specialized meanings later developed from the idea of something long, projecting, or forceful.
boom.explanation: Refers to a deep, loud, resonant sound or to a period of rapid growth, prosperity, or increased activity. It can also mean a long projecting pole on a crane, sailboat, microphone stand, or similar device, or a floating barrier placed across water. As a verb, boom means to make a deep loud sound or to grow rapidly and successfully.

senses.definition: Noun: a deep, loud, resonant sound.
examples: A loud boom shook the windows.
They heard the boom of thunder in the distance.
The explosion produced a tremendous boom.

senses.definition: Noun: a period of rapid economic growth, prosperity, or increased activity.
examples: The region experienced an economic boom.
A construction boom transformed the downtown area.
The technology boom created thousands of new jobs.

senses.definition: Noun: a sudden or rapid increase in popularity, demand, production, or population.
examples: The city experienced a tourism boom.
There was a boom in demand for electric vehicles.
The postwar period brought a major population boom.

senses.definition: Noun: a long projecting pole or arm used on a crane, sailboat, microphone support, or similar equipment.
examples: The crane's boom extended over the construction site.
The sailor adjusted the boom on the sailboat.
The sound technician positioned the microphone boom above the actors.

senses.definition: Noun: a floating barrier used to control, contain, or block objects or substances on water.
examples: Workers placed a boom around the oil spill.
The floating boom prevented debris from reaching the harbor.
A containment boom was deployed across the inlet.

senses.definition: Verb: to make a deep, loud, resonant sound.
examples: Thunder boomed across the valley.
The cannon boomed in the distance.
His voice boomed through the auditorium.

senses.definition: Verb: to grow, expand, or prosper rapidly.
examples: Business boomed during the summer.
The city's population boomed after the new factories opened.
Online shopping boomed during the decade.

boost.etymology: Probably of American English origin in the nineteenth century, initially referring to pushing or lifting something upward; the word later developed broader senses involving increases, improvements, and added support.
boost.explanation: As a verb, boost means to increase, improve, strengthen, promote, or lift something. As a noun, a boost is an increase, improvement, encouragement, or added amount of power or support.

senses.definition: Verb: to increase the amount, level, strength, value, or effectiveness of something.
examples: The company hopes to boost sales with the new product.
Regular exercise can boost energy levels.
The investment helped boost production.

senses.definition: Verb: to improve someone's confidence, morale, reputation, or chances of success.
examples: The encouraging news boosted her confidence.
The victory boosted the team's morale.
Positive reviews helped boost the author's reputation.

senses.definition: Verb: to promote, advertise, or support someone or something.
examples: The campaign was designed to boost local tourism.
The organization boosted the event through social media.
Officials introduced measures to boost small businesses.

senses.definition: Verb: to lift or push someone or something upward.
examples: He boosted the child over the fence.
She gave him a boost onto the platform.
They boosted the equipment into the truck.

senses.definition: Noun: an increase or improvement in amount, strength, value, performance, or activity.
examples: The tax reduction gave the economy a boost.
Sales received a boost during the holiday season.
The new equipment provided a significant boost in productivity.

senses.definition: Noun: encouragement or support that improves confidence, morale, or prospects.
examples: The award gave her confidence a major boost.
The team's victory provided a much-needed morale boost.
His recommendation gave the project an important boost.

senses.definition: Noun: a push or lift that helps someone or something move upward.
examples: He gave her a boost over the wall.
The child needed a boost to reach the shelf.
She asked for a boost onto the horse.

senses.definition: Noun: an added amount of power, energy, or signal strength.
examples: The engine received an extra boost of power.
The amplifier gives the signal a boost.
A strong tailwind gave the aircraft an additional boost.

boot.etymology: From Old French bote, meaning a type of footwear. The computing sense developed much later from bootstrap, referring to the process by which a computer loads the instructions needed to start itself.
boot.explanation: Refers primarily to a sturdy item of footwear that covers the foot and extends above the ankle. As a verb, boot can mean to kick something, to start a computer or operating system, or informally to force someone to leave. In British English, boot can also mean the enclosed storage compartment of a car.
usageNotes: In computing, boot means to start a computer and load its operating system.
In British English, the boot of a car is what American English usually calls the trunk.

senses.definition: Noun: a sturdy item of footwear that covers the foot and extends above the ankle.
examples: He wore heavy boots in the snow.
She bought a new pair of hiking boots.
Mud covered the bottom of his boot.

senses.definition: Noun, British English: the enclosed storage compartment of a car; the trunk.
examples: She placed the groceries in the boot.
The spare tire is stored in the boot.
He opened the boot to remove the luggage.

senses.definition: Verb: to kick someone or something, especially forcefully.
examples: He booted the ball across the field.
She booted the door shut.
The player booted the ball toward the goal.

senses.definition: Verb, computing: to start a computer or device and load the software required for operation.
examples: The computer takes several seconds to boot.
She booted the system from an external drive.
The machine failed to boot after the update.

senses.definition: Verb, informal: to remove, dismiss, or force someone to leave a place, position, group, or system.
examples: The manager booted him from the meeting.
The player was booted from the game.
The administrator booted the inactive user from the server.

booth.etymology: From Middle English bothe, from Old Norse buth, meaning a temporary shelter, dwelling, shop, or stall
booth.explanation: Refers to a small enclosed or partly enclosed space designed for a particular activity. A booth may be used for selling goods, displaying information, providing privacy, seating customers, voting, making calls, recording sound, or performing other specialized functions.

senses.definition: A small stall or enclosed space used for selling goods, providing services, or displaying information.
examples: They purchased food from a booth at the festival.
The company set up a booth at the trade show.
Volunteers staffed an information booth near the entrance.

senses.definition: A small enclosed or partly enclosed space designed to provide privacy for a particular activity.
examples: She entered the voting booth to mark her ballot.
He made the call from a telephone booth.
The singer recorded the vocals inside a soundproof booth.

senses.definition: A seating area in a restaurant consisting of a table with fixed or high-backed seats, usually providing more privacy than ordinary tables.
examples: We asked for a booth near the window.
The family sat together in a large booth.
The restaurant has both booths and regular tables.

senses.definition: A small compartment or station from which a person performs a specialized job or controls equipment.
examples: The operator worked from a booth overlooking the entrance.
Tickets were sold from a booth outside the stadium.
The announcer watched the game from the broadcast booth.

border.etymology: From Old French bordure, meaning edge, boundary, or margin, from bord, meaning edge or side
border.explanation: Refers to a boundary or dividing line between places, regions, countries, or areas, or to the outer edge of an object or surface. It can also mean a decorative band around something. As a verb, border means to lie next to a boundary, share a boundary with another place, or form an edge around something.

senses.definition: Noun: the boundary or dividing line between two countries, states, regions, or other geographic areas.
examples: They crossed the border into the neighboring country.
The river forms part of the state border.
Officials increased security along the border.

senses.definition: Noun: the outer edge or margin of an object, surface, or area.
examples: A narrow path runs along the border of the field.
She drew a line around the border of the page.
Flowers grew along the garden border.

senses.definition: Noun: a decorative band, pattern, or strip placed around the edge of something.
examples: The rug has a red and gold border.
She added a decorative border to the invitation.
The photograph was surrounded by a black border.

senses.definition: Verb: to share a boundary with or lie next to another place or area.
examples: Canada borders the United States.
The property borders a large public park.
Several farms border the river.

senses.definition: Verb: to form an edge or boundary around something.
examples: Tall trees border the road.
A stone wall borders the garden.
Mountains border the valley on both sides.

senses.definition: Verb: to approach or nearly reach a particular condition, quality, or state.
examples: His behavior bordered on disrespect.
The situation bordered on chaos.
Her excitement bordered on disbelief.

bore.etymology: The drilling sense comes from Old English borian, meaning to bore, pierce, or make a hole. The sense meaning to weary through dullness developed later and may have a separate origin. Bore is also the past tense of bear, from a different historical source.
bore.explanation: As a verb, bore can mean to make a hole by drilling or cutting, or to make someone feel uninterested or weary through dullness or repetition. As a noun, a bore can be a drilled hole, the internal diameter of a tube or cylinder, or a dull and tiresome person or situation. Bore is also the simple past tense of the separate verb bear.
usageNotes: Bore is also the simple past tense of bear, as in 'She bore the burden patiently' or 'The tree bore fruit.' That use belongs to the lemma bear rather than to this lexical entry.
In descriptions of firearms, engines, pipes, and similar objects, bore can refer to the interior diameter or internal passage.

relatedWords.relationship: Separate verb for which bore is the past tense

senses.definition: Verb: to make a hole in something by drilling, cutting, or piercing.
examples: Workers bored a hole through the wall.
The machine can bore through solid rock.
He carefully bored into the wooden panel.

senses.definition: Verb: to make someone feel uninterested, weary, or impatient because something is dull or repetitive.
examples: The long speech bored the audience.
He worried that the technical details would bore his readers.
The repetitive task quickly bored her.

senses.definition: Noun: a hole or passage made by drilling or boring.
examples: The engineer inspected the bore in the metal block.
Water flowed through the narrow bore.
The drill produced a clean, straight bore.

senses.definition: Noun: the internal diameter or interior passage of a tube, pipe, cylinder, barrel, or similar object.
examples: The pipe has a relatively narrow bore.
The engine cylinder has a larger bore than the previous model.
The technician measured the bore of the tube.

senses.definition: Noun: a person who is dull, tedious, or tiresome to be around.
examples: He can be a bore when he talks only about himself.
She feared that the guest would think her a bore.
The character is portrayed as an arrogant bore.

senses.definition: Noun: something dull, tedious, or inconvenient.
examples: Filling out the paperwork was a bore.
The long delay became a real bore.
Cleaning the storage room is always a bore.

bored.etymology: Formed from bore with the adjective-forming use of the past participle ending -ed, describing someone affected by boredom or lack of interest
bored.explanation: Describes someone who feels uninterested, weary, or restless because an activity, situation, or experience is dull, repetitive, or lacking in stimulation. Bored describes the person experiencing the feeling, while boring usually describes the thing that causes it.
usageNotes: Bored describes the person or animal experiencing a lack of interest, while boring describes the person, activity, or thing causing that feeling. For example, 'I am bored' means I feel uninterested, while 'The lecture is boring' means the lecture causes boredom.
Bored is also the past tense and past participle of bore when bore means to make someone uninterested or to drill a hole.

senses.definition: Feeling uninterested, weary, or restless because something is dull, repetitive, or lacking in stimulation.
examples: The children became bored during the long wait.
She felt bored after spending the entire afternoon indoors.
He quickly grew bored with the repetitive task.

senses.definition: Having lost interest in a particular activity, subject, person, or situation.
examples: She was bored with the television program.
He became bored with doing the same work every day.
The students looked bored with the discussion.

boredom.etymology: Formed from bore with the noun-forming suffix -dom, referring to the state or condition of being bored
boredom.explanation: Refers to the unpleasant feeling of being uninterested, unstimulated, or weary because an activity, situation, or period of time seems dull, repetitive, or lacking in meaningful engagement.

senses.definition: The state or feeling of being uninterested, weary, or restless because something is dull or lacking in stimulation.
examples: The children complained of boredom during the long trip.
She read a book to relieve her boredom.
Hours of waiting produced growing boredom among the passengers.

senses.definition: A lack of interest or engagement caused by repetition, inactivity, or insufficient mental or physical stimulation.
examples: Repetitive work can lead to boredom.
He changed hobbies whenever boredom began to set in.
The program was designed to prevent boredom by offering a variety of activities.

boring.etymology: Formed from bore with the suffix -ing. The adjective developed from the participial sense of something that causes boredom, while the noun can refer to the act or process of making a hole by drilling or cutting.
boring.explanation: As an adjective, boring describes someone or something that causes boredom because it is dull, repetitive, predictable, or lacking in interest. As a noun, boring can refer to the act or process of drilling, cutting, or making a hole in a material.
usageNotes: Boring describes the person, activity, or thing that causes boredom, while bored describes the person or animal experiencing the feeling. For example, 'The lecture is boring' means the lecture causes boredom, while 'I am bored' means I feel uninterested.
Boring is also the present participle and gerund form of the verb bore.

senses.definition: Adjective: causing boredom because something is dull, repetitive, predictable, or lacking in interest.
examples: The lecture was boring and difficult to follow.
He found the repetitive work extremely boring.
The movie became boring after the first hour.

senses.definition: Adjective: lacking qualities that attract, hold, or stimulate attention.
examples: She thought the conversation was boring.
The textbook would be less boring with more illustrations.
He worried that his presentation might sound boring.

senses.definition: Noun: the act or process of making a hole by drilling, cutting, or piercing.
examples: The boring of the tunnel continued throughout the year.
Special equipment was used for boring through the rock.
The project required deep boring beneath the site.

senses.definition: Noun, usually plural: material removed while drilling or boring a hole.
examples: Metal borings collected beneath the machine.
The workers cleared the wood borings from the floor.
Samples of the drill borings were sent for analysis.

born.etymology: Originally the past participle of bear in the sense of giving birth, from Old English beran, meaning to carry, bear, or bring forth
born.explanation: Describes a person or animal as having come into life through birth. It can also describe qualities, abilities, or characteristics that appear natural or present from birth. Although born developed from the verb bear, it functions independently in many common expressions.
usageNotes: Born is used as the past participle of bear when referring to birth, especially in the passive construction 'was born.'
Borne is generally used instead of born for other past-participle meanings of bear, as in 'The cost was borne by the company' or 'The disease is mosquito-borne.'
Born commonly appears before a noun in expressions describing natural ability or identity, such as 'a born leader.'

senses.definition: Having come into life through birth.
examples: She was born in Seattle.
The baby was born early in the morning.
He was born into a large family.

senses.definition: Originating from or belonging to a particular place from birth.
examples: She is a California-born writer.
He was born and raised in Chicago.
The locally born residents knew the region well.

senses.definition: Having a natural ability, quality, tendency, or characteristic that appears to have been present from birth.
examples: She is a born leader.
He seemed to be a born musician.
The child was a born storyteller.

senses.definition: Coming into existence or developing from a particular circumstance, idea, or experience.
examples: The organization was born from a desire to improve the community.
Their partnership was born out of necessity.
The idea was born during a late-night discussion.

borough.etymology: From Old English burg or burh, meaning a fortified place, town, or settlement, related to words such as bury and burg
borough.explanation: Refers to a town, municipality, or administrative district having a particular form of local government. The precise meaning varies by country and jurisdiction. In New York City, for example, borough refers to each of the city's five major geographic and administrative divisions.
usageNotes: The legal and administrative meaning of borough varies considerably between jurisdictions.
New York City consists of five boroughs: Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx, and Staten Island.

senses.definition: A town, municipality, or other incorporated area having a particular form of local government.
examples: The borough elected a new mayor.
Local services are administered by the borough government.
She attended a public meeting at the borough hall.

senses.definition: An administrative or geographic division within a larger city or region.
examples: Brooklyn is a borough of New York City.
Each borough has its own distinctive neighborhoods.
The transportation plan affects residents throughout the borough.

senses.definition: In Britain, historically and in certain modern governmental arrangements, a town or district granted a particular municipal or administrative status.
examples: The town received borough status centuries ago.
The council administers services throughout the borough.
Several surrounding communities are included within the borough.

borrow.etymology: From Old English borgian, meaning to borrow, pledge, or obtain on security, related to words involving guarantees and obligations
borrow.explanation: Means to receive or use something temporarily with the expectation that it will be returned, replaced, or repaid. It commonly refers to money, objects, or resources, but can also describe taking words, ideas, styles, or features from another language, culture, or source.
usageNotes: Borrow describes receiving something temporarily, while lend describes giving something temporarily. For example, 'Can I borrow your pen?' and 'Can you lend me your pen?' express the same transaction from opposite perspectives.

senses.definition: To receive and use something temporarily with the intention of returning it.
examples: She borrowed a book from the library.
Can I borrow your pen for a moment?
He borrowed his neighbor's ladder.

senses.definition: To receive money with an obligation to repay it, usually under agreed terms.
examples: They borrowed money to purchase the house.
The company borrowed funds from the bank.
She borrowed five thousand dollars to start the business.

senses.definition: To take or adopt a word, expression, idea, style, method, or feature from another source.
examples: English has borrowed many words from French.
The architect borrowed ideas from classical design.
The film borrows several elements from earlier stories.

borrower.etymology: Formed from borrow with the agent-forming suffix -er, meaning a person or organization that borrows something
borrower.explanation: Refers to a person, organization, or other entity that receives money, property, or another resource temporarily with an obligation or expectation to return, replace, or repay it. The term is especially common in banking, lending, and finance.

senses.definition: A person who receives and temporarily uses something belonging to someone else with the expectation of returning it.
examples: The borrower returned the book to the library.
Each borrower is responsible for returning the equipment on time.
The lender asked the borrower to take good care of the tools.

senses.definition: A person, business, government, or other entity that receives money as a loan and is obligated to repay it.
examples: The borrower must repay the loan with interest.
The bank reviewed the borrower's credit history.
Borrowers should understand the terms of a loan before signing the agreement.

boss.etymology: From Dutch baas, meaning master, overseer, or person in charge. The word became common in American English as a less formal alternative to master.
boss.explanation: Refers to a person who supervises, manages, directs, or has authority over other people, especially in a workplace. It can also describe a powerful political or organizational leader. As a verb, boss means to give orders or direct someone, often in an overly controlling manner.

senses.definition: Noun: a person who supervises, manages, or has authority over workers or employees.
examples: She asked her boss for the day off.
The boss called a meeting with the entire staff.
He has worked for the same boss for several years.

senses.definition: Noun: a person who exercises strong control or authority within an organization, group, or political system.
examples: The local political boss controlled many appointments.
He became the undisputed boss of the organization.
The party boss had considerable influence over local elections.

senses.definition: Verb: to direct, order, or control someone.
examples: She bosses the crew during the morning shift.
He tried to boss everyone around.
The older child kept bossing his younger brother.

both.etymology: From Middle English bothe, from Old Norse bathir, meaning the two together or each of two
both.explanation: Refers to two people, things, groups, or qualities considered together. As a determiner, both comes before a plural noun or another determiner. As a pronoun, it stands for two previously identified people or things. In the paired construction 'both ... and ...,' it joins two equally included elements.
usageNotes: Both refers specifically to two people or things, not to groups of three or more.
The construction 'both ... and ...' emphasizes that two people, things, qualities, or actions are equally included, as in 'both large and expensive.'
Both normally takes a plural verb when it functions as a pronoun, as in 'Both are correct.'

senses.definition: Determiner: the two people or things considered together.
examples: Both students passed the examination.
She held a bag in both hands.
Both houses were damaged by the storm.

senses.definition: Pronoun: the two people or things previously mentioned or understood.
examples: I invited Anna and David, and both accepted.
There were two possible answers, but both were correct.
Both of them arrived early.

senses.definition: Determiner: each of two people, things, sides, or parts.
examples: There are shops on both sides of the street.
Both ends of the rope were secured.
The agreement benefits both parties.

senses.definition: Conjunction, in the construction 'both ... and ...': used to connect and emphasize two equally included words, phrases, or clauses.
examples: She is both intelligent and hardworking.
The program serves both children and adults.
He both wrote and directed the film.

bother.etymology: Of uncertain origin, first recorded in English in the eighteenth century with senses involving confusion, disturbance, annoyance, and trouble
bother.explanation: As a verb, bother means to annoy, disturb, inconvenience, worry, or trouble someone. It can also mean to make the effort to do something, especially when the action seems difficult, unnecessary, or inconvenient. As a noun, bother refers to trouble, annoyance, difficulty, or inconvenience.
usageNotes: The expression 'don't bother' can mean either 'do not trouble or disturb someone' or 'do not make the effort,' depending on context.
Bother is commonly followed by an infinitive or gerund, as in 'He didn't bother to call' and 'Don't bother asking.'

senses.definition: Verb: to annoy, disturb, interrupt, or inconvenience someone.
examples: The noise from the hallway bothered her.
Please do not bother him while he is working.
The mosquitoes bothered us throughout the evening.

senses.definition: Verb: to cause someone worry, concern, discomfort, or emotional distress.
examples: The unanswered question continued to bother him.
It bothers me that no one reported the problem.
Her knee has been bothering her for several days.

senses.definition: Verb: to make the effort or take the trouble to do something.
examples: He did not bother to read the instructions.
She bothered to call and explain what happened.
Don't bother bringing food because dinner is already prepared.

senses.definition: Noun: trouble, annoyance, inconvenience, or difficulty.
examples: The repair caused more bother than expected.
I hope the change does not create too much bother.
She completed the task without much bother.

senses.definition: Noun: a person, thing, or situation that causes annoyance or difficulty.
examples: The broken lock became a constant bother.
Traveling with so much luggage was a bother.
The paperwork was a minor bother compared with the rest of the process.

bottle.etymology: From Old French boteille, meaning bottle or container, from Late Latin butticula, a diminutive of buttis, meaning cask or vessel
bottle.explanation: Refers to a container, usually made of glass or plastic, with a narrow neck and an opening that can be closed with a cap, cork, or other stopper. Bottles are commonly used to hold liquids such as water, milk, medicine, or beverages. As a verb, bottle means to put a liquid or other substance into bottles, or figuratively to suppress feelings instead of expressing them.

senses.definition: Noun: a container, usually with a narrow neck, used for storing or transporting liquids.
examples: She filled the bottle with water.
The medicine comes in a small glass bottle.
He placed the empty bottles in the recycling bin.

senses.definition: Noun: the amount of liquid contained in a bottle.
examples: They drank a bottle of water during the hike.
She bought two bottles of juice.
The recipe calls for one bottle of sauce.

senses.definition: Verb: to place or package a liquid or other substance in bottles.
examples: The company bottles spring water at the plant.
They bottled the homemade juice for later use.
The sauce is bottled immediately after cooking.

senses.definition: Verb, figurative: to suppress or contain an emotion instead of expressing it.
examples: He tends to bottle up his anger.
She bottled her feelings for years.
It can be difficult to keep frustration bottled up.

bottom.etymology: From Old English botm, meaning the lowest part, foundation, ground, or base, from a Germanic source
bottom.explanation: Refers to the lowest, deepest, or supporting part of something. It can describe the lower surface of an object, the lowest point of a container or body of water, the final position in a ranking, or the underlying cause of a problem. As an adjective, bottom means lowest or situated beneath others. As a verb, bottom means to reach the lowest point before stabilizing or rising.

senses.definition: Noun: the lowest part, point, or surface of something.
examples: The keys were at the bottom of the bag.
She signed her name at the bottom of the page.
Mud covered the bottom of the pond.

senses.definition: Noun: the supporting or lower surface of an object or container.
examples: The bottom of the box was damaged.
A small hole appeared in the bottom of the bucket.
The pan has a thick metal bottom.

senses.definition: Noun: the lowest position in a ranking, scale, list, or organization.
examples: The team finished at the bottom of the standings.
His name appeared near the bottom of the list.
The company fell to the bottom of the industry rankings.

senses.definition: Noun: the buttocks or the part of the body on which a person sits.
examples: The child fell and landed on his bottom.
She sat down on the floor with her bottom against the wall.
The pants were torn near the bottom.

senses.definition: Noun: the fundamental cause, truth, or explanation underlying a situation or problem.
examples: Investigators tried to get to the bottom of the problem.
No one knew what was really at the bottom of the dispute.
The audit helped uncover the issue at the bottom of the losses.

senses.definition: Adjective: situated at the lowest position or level.
examples: The books are stored on the bottom shelf.
She opened the bottom drawer.
The bottom floor was used for storage.

senses.definition: Adjective: lowest in rank, amount, quality, or position.
examples: The company entered the bottom half of the rankings.
Students in the bottom group received additional instruction.
The bottom score was removed from the final calculation.

senses.definition: Verb: to reach the lowest point or level before becoming stable or beginning to rise.
examples: Prices appeared to bottom during the summer.
The market bottomed before beginning a gradual recovery.
Sales bottomed out in March and improved afterward.

bounce.etymology: Probably imitative in origin, reflecting the sound or motion of something striking a surface and springing back
bounce.explanation: As a verb, bounce means to strike a surface and spring back, to move up and down repeatedly, or to cause something to do so. It can also mean to recover quickly, return a message or payment because it cannot be processed, or informally to remove someone from a place. As a noun, a bounce is a rebound, springing movement, or sudden recovery.

senses.definition: Verb: to strike a surface and spring or move back from it.
examples: The ball bounced off the wall.
The stone bounced across the pavement.
The basketball bounced several times before stopping.

senses.definition: Verb: to move repeatedly up and down or cause something to move in this way.
examples: The child bounced on the bed.
She bounced the baby gently on her knee.
The truck bounced over the rough road.

senses.definition: Verb: to recover quickly from a setback, illness, loss, or difficult situation.
examples: The company bounced back after a difficult year.
She quickly bounced back from the disappointment.
Sales bounced after several months of decline.

senses.definition: Verb: for a check, payment, email, or other communication to be returned or rejected because it cannot be processed or delivered.
examples: The check bounced because there was not enough money in the account.
My email bounced back because the address was incorrect.
The payment bounced after the bank rejected the transaction.

senses.definition: Verb, informal: to remove, eject, or force someone to leave a place.
examples: Security bounced him from the club.
The moderator bounced the disruptive user from the chat.
They were bounced from the event after causing trouble.

senses.definition: Noun: a movement in which something strikes a surface and springs back.
examples: The ball took a strange bounce.
One high bounce carried the ball over the fence.
The uneven floor caused an unpredictable bounce.

senses.definition: Noun: a quick recovery, increase, or return to a stronger condition.
examples: The market experienced a brief bounce after the decline.
The team hoped for a bounce in performance.
Sales showed a noticeable bounce during the holiday season.

bound.etymology: Bound has several historical sources. The adjective meaning tied or obligated developed from the past participle of bind. The sense meaning destined or headed toward a place is related to an older word meaning prepared or ready. The noun and verb senses involving limits and leaping developed through separate historical paths.
bound.explanation: Bound has several distinct meanings. As an adjective, it can mean tied or fastened, required by an obligation, certain or very likely to happen, or traveling toward a destination. As a noun, a bound can be a limit or a leap. As a verb, bound means to move forward with large energetic leaps. Bound is also the past tense and past participle of the separate verb bind.
usageNotes: Bound is the past tense and past participle of bind, as in 'The ropes bound the package tightly.' That grammatical use belongs to the lemma bind.
In the expression 'bound to,' bound means certain or very likely, as in 'The plan is bound to change.'
When followed by 'for,' bound commonly means traveling toward a destination, as in 'a train bound for Chicago.'

relatedWords.relationship: Separate verb for which bound is the past tense and past participle

senses.definition: Adjective: tied, fastened, secured, or held together.
examples: The documents were bound together with string.
The prisoner remained bound at the wrists.
The book was bound in leather.

senses.definition: Adjective: required or obligated by law, agreement, duty, promise, or circumstance.
examples: Both parties are bound by the contract.
Employees are bound to follow the safety rules.
She felt bound by her promise.

senses.definition: Adjective: certain or very likely to happen, occur, or produce a particular result.
examples: Mistakes are bound to happen occasionally.
The new policy is bound to attract attention.
Prices are bound to change over time.

senses.definition: Adjective: traveling or directed toward a particular destination.
examples: They boarded a train bound for Seattle.
The ship was bound for Europe.
Northbound traffic was delayed by the accident.

senses.definition: Noun: a limit, boundary, or restriction beyond which something should not or cannot go, especially in the plural.
examples: His behavior went beyond the bounds of acceptable conduct.
The discussion remained within reasonable bounds.
The property lies outside the city bounds.

senses.definition: Noun: a long or energetic leap.
examples: The dog crossed the yard in a single bound.
The deer escaped with several powerful bounds.
She cleared the obstacle with one quick bound.

senses.definition: Verb: to move forward with large, energetic leaps or jumps.
examples: The dog bounded across the field.
The deer bounded into the forest.
She bounded up the stairs when she heard the news.

boundary.etymology: Formed from bound, meaning a limit or border, with the noun-forming suffix -ary
boundary.explanation: Refers to a line, edge, or limit that marks where one area, property, region, or concept ends and another begins. The word can describe physical borders as well as legal, social, personal, or conceptual limits.

senses.definition: A line or edge marking the limit of an area, property, region, or territory.
examples: A fence marks the boundary between the two properties.
The river forms the northern boundary of the county.
Surveyors identified the exact property boundary.

senses.definition: A limit beyond which something does not or should not extend.
examples: The project remained within the agreed boundaries.
The law establishes clear boundaries on government authority.
Scientific inquiry often pushes the boundaries of existing knowledge.

senses.definition: A social, personal, ethical, or behavioral limit that defines acceptable interaction or conduct.
examples: She established clear boundaries between work and personal life.
Healthy relationships require respect for personal boundaries.
The manager reminded employees to maintain professional boundaries.

senses.definition: A dividing point or distinction between two ideas, categories, conditions, or fields.
examples: The technology blurs the boundary between work and entertainment.
The course examines the boundary between science and philosophy.
The case tested the boundary between lawful protest and unlawful conduct.

bow.etymology: Bow represents several historically related and unrelated senses. The pronunciation BOH, referring to a curved weapon, ribbon knot, or similar curved object, comes largely from Old English boga, meaning bow or arch. The pronunciation BOW, meaning to bend the body or referring to the front of a ship, developed through separate Germanic and nautical histories.
bow.explanation: Bow is a heteronym with two common pronunciations and several meanings. Pronounced BOH, it can refer to a curved weapon used to shoot arrows, a decorative knot made from ribbon, or a curved implement used to play stringed instruments. Pronounced BOW, it means to bend the head or upper body as a sign of respect or acknowledgment and can also refer to the front part of a ship or boat.
usageNotes: Bow is a heteronym. It is pronounced BOH (boʊ) when referring to an archery weapon, ribbon knot, or the implement used to play certain stringed instruments.
Bow is pronounced BOW (baʊ), rhyming with 'cow,' when it means to bend the head or body or when it refers to the front of a ship or boat.
