senses.definition: Noun, pronounced BOH: a curved weapon with a tightly stretched string, used for shooting arrows.
examples: The archer raised his bow and aimed at the target.
She learned to shoot a bow at summer camp.
The museum displayed an ancient wooden bow.

senses.definition: Noun, pronounced BOH: a decorative knot with two loops, usually made from ribbon, fabric, or another flexible material.
examples: She tied a red bow around the gift.
The child wore a blue bow in her hair.
A large ribbon bow decorated the package.

senses.definition: Noun, pronounced BOH: a long, slender implement with stretched horsehair or synthetic fibers used to play certain stringed instruments.
examples: The violinist drew the bow across the strings.
She tightened the hair on her bow before the performance.
The cello bow rested beside the instrument.

senses.definition: Verb, pronounced BOW: to bend the head or upper body forward as a sign of respect, greeting, gratitude, submission, or acknowledgment.
examples: The performers bowed to the audience.
He bowed politely before leaving the room.
The students bowed their heads during the ceremony.

senses.definition: Noun, pronounced BOW: an act of bending the head or upper body forward.
examples: The actor gave a final bow after the performance.
She greeted the guests with a slight bow.
He acknowledged the applause with a deep bow.

senses.definition: Noun, pronounced BOW: the front part of a ship, boat, or other vessel.
examples: She stood near the bow of the ship.
Waves crashed against the boat's bow.
The passengers gathered at the bow to watch the coastline.

senses.definition: Verb, pronounced BOW: to bend, curve, or cause something to bend downward or outward.
examples: The heavy snow bowed the branches toward the ground.
The wooden shelf began to bow under the weight.
The pressure caused the panel to bow outward.

bowl.etymology: The noun comes from Old English bolla, meaning a rounded vessel or cup. The verb associated with rolling a ball developed from the use of bowls in games.
bowl.explanation: Refers primarily to a deep, rounded container used for holding or serving food, liquids, or other materials. It can also refer to the amount such a container holds, a rounded or bowl-shaped part of something, or a large stadium. As a verb, bowl means to roll or throw a ball, especially in bowling, cricket, or similar games.

senses.definition: Noun: a deep, usually round container used for holding, preparing, or serving food, liquids, or other substances.
examples: She poured the soup into a bowl.
The fruit was arranged in a large wooden bowl.
He mixed the ingredients in a glass bowl.

senses.definition: Noun: the amount of food, liquid, or other material contained in a bowl.
examples: He ate a bowl of cereal for breakfast.
She ordered a bowl of soup.
The child finished two bowls of ice cream.

senses.definition: Noun: a rounded or hollow part of an object resembling a bowl.
examples: The spoon has a deep bowl.
Water collected in the bowl of the fountain.
The pipe has a small bowl for holding tobacco.

senses.definition: Noun: a large stadium or arena, especially one with seating arranged around a central field.
examples: Thousands of fans filled the bowl for the championship game.
The stadium bowl provides an excellent view from most seats.
The concert was held in a large outdoor bowl.

senses.definition: Verb: to roll a ball toward pins or another target, especially in the game of bowling.
examples: She bowled the ball straight down the lane.
They bowl together every Friday night.
He bowled a strike on his final turn.

senses.definition: Verb, cricket: to deliver the ball toward the batter.
examples: The player bowled a fast delivery.
She bowled accurately throughout the match.
He was chosen to bowl the final over.

senses.definition: Verb: to move rapidly and smoothly, especially on wheels.
examples: The car bowled along the highway.
They bowled down the road toward the coast.
The cyclist came bowling around the corner.

bowling.etymology: Formed from bowl with the noun-forming suffix -ing, originally referring to the act of rolling a ball in a game
bowling.explanation: Refers primarily to games or sports in which a ball is rolled toward pins, smaller balls, or another target. In cricket, bowling refers to the act or skill of delivering the ball toward the batter. Bowling is also the present participle and gerund form of the verb bowl.
usageNotes: In American English, bowling without additional qualification most commonly refers to ten-pin bowling.
Bowling is also the present participle and gerund form of the verb bowl.

senses.definition: A sport or recreational game in which a player rolls a ball along a lane toward a group of pins.
examples: They went bowling after dinner.
Bowling is a popular recreational activity.
She joined a bowling league with several coworkers.

senses.definition: The act or activity of rolling a ball toward pins or another target in a bowling game.
examples: His bowling improved with regular practice.
The instructor demonstrated proper bowling technique.
Accurate bowling requires control of both speed and direction.

senses.definition: A group of related games in which balls are rolled toward a target, including ten-pin bowling and lawn bowls.
examples: Different forms of bowling are played around the world.
The recreation center offers both indoor and outdoor bowling.
The history of bowling extends back many centuries.

senses.definition: In cricket, the act, technique, or performance of delivering the ball toward the batter.
examples: Her fast bowling troubled the opposing batters.
The team relied on strong bowling throughout the match.
His bowling became more accurate during the second innings.

box.etymology: From Old English box, from Latin buxus, referring originally to the box tree and objects made from its wood. The verb meaning to fight with the fists developed separately through the sport of boxing.
box.explanation: Refers primarily to a container with flat sides, usually square or rectangular, used for storing, carrying, or protecting objects. It can also mean an enclosed area, compartment, or designated space. As a verb, box means to place something in a box, enclose or restrict something, or fight using the fists according to the rules of boxing.

senses.definition: Noun: a container, usually square or rectangular, with flat sides and often a lid.
examples: She packed the books into a cardboard box.
The gift arrived in a small box.
He stored the tools in a wooden box.

senses.definition: Noun: the amount or quantity contained in a box.
examples: She bought a box of cereal.
He ate nearly an entire box of cookies.
The office ordered several boxes of paper.

senses.definition: Noun: an enclosed or clearly defined space, compartment, or area.
examples: Write your answer in the box provided.
The theater has a private box overlooking the stage.
The electrical controls are housed inside a metal box.

senses.definition: Noun: a square or rectangular area used to organize information on a page, screen, form, or diagram.
examples: Check the box beside the correct answer.
Enter your address in the box at the top of the form.
The diagram places each step inside a separate box.

senses.definition: Verb: to place, pack, or store something in a box.
examples: They boxed the equipment for shipping.
She boxed the books before moving.
Workers boxed the finished products at the factory.

senses.definition: Verb: to enclose, confine, or restrict someone or something within a limited space or situation.
examples: The parked cars boxed him in.
She felt boxed in by the narrow office.
The opposing players boxed the defender into the corner.

senses.definition: Verb: to fight another person with the fists, especially according to the rules of the sport of boxing.
examples: He boxed professionally for several years.
The two athletes boxed for three rounds.
She learned to box at a local gym.

boxer.etymology: Formed from box with the agent-forming suffix -er, referring to a person who boxes. The name of the Boxer dog breed developed separately in German.
boxer.explanation: Refers primarily to a person who participates in the sport of boxing. Boxer is also the name of a muscular, short-haired breed of dog. In the plural form boxers, the word commonly refers to loose-fitting men's underwear known as boxer shorts.
usageNotes: The plural boxers commonly refers to boxer shorts, a loose-fitting style of underwear.
Boxer is usually capitalized when referring specifically to the recognized dog breed.

senses.definition: A person who participates in boxing, especially as an amateur or professional athlete.
examples: The boxer trained every morning before the fight.
She became a professional boxer after winning several amateur titles.
The boxer defended himself carefully during the final round.

senses.definition: A medium-to-large, muscular breed of dog with a short coat and broad muzzle.
examples: Their Boxer is energetic and friendly.
The Boxer was originally developed as a working dog.
She adopted a young Boxer from the shelter.

senses.definition: Usually plural, boxers: loose-fitting underwear with short legs, traditionally worn by men.
examples: He bought a new pair of boxers.
The store sells boxers in several patterns.
He packed socks and boxers for the trip.

boxing.etymology: Formed from box with the noun-forming suffix -ing, referring to the act or sport of fighting with the fists according to established rules
boxing.explanation: Refers primarily to a combat sport in which two competitors fight with their fists while wearing padded gloves and following established rules. Boxing involves techniques such as punching, blocking, footwork, and defensive movement. The word is also the present participle and gerund form of the verb box.
usageNotes: Boxing is also the present participle and gerund form of the verb box.
Competitive boxing is generally divided into amateur and professional forms, with rules varying by organization and competition.

senses.definition: A combat sport in which two competitors use their fists to strike one another while following established rules and wearing protective gloves.
examples: He began training in boxing as a teenager.
Boxing requires strength, speed, endurance, and defensive skill.
She won a national championship in amateur boxing.

senses.definition: The activity, practice, or technique of fighting with the fists according to the methods and rules of boxing.
examples: The gym offers boxing classes several evenings each week.
Good boxing depends heavily on footwork and timing.
He practices boxing to improve his fitness and coordination.

boy.etymology: From Middle English boy, meaning a male servant or young male; its earlier origin is uncertain. The modern sense of a male child developed during the Middle English period.
boy.explanation: Refers primarily to a male child or young male person. It can also mean a son, a young man, or informally a male friend or member of a group. Historically, boy has sometimes been used to address adult men in a belittling or discriminatory way, particularly Black men in the United States.
usageNotes: Boy most commonly refers to a male child or adolescent.
When referring to an adult man, boy can sound overly familiar, dismissive, or insulting depending on context.

In the United States, calling an adult Black man 'boy' has a documented history as a racist and demeaning form of address associated with slavery, segregation, and assertions of racial hierarchy. Context is therefore especially important in this use.

senses.definition: A male child or adolescent.
examples: The boy rode his bicycle to school.
A young boy was playing in the park.
The boys formed a line outside the classroom.

senses.definition: A person's male child; a son.
examples: They have two boys and one girl.
Their oldest boy started college this year.
She watched proudly as her boy received the award.

senses.definition: A young man, especially one who is not yet regarded as fully mature.
examples: He was still a boy when he began working on the farm.
The boys joined the team after graduating from school.
She remembered him as a quiet boy who loved books.

senses.definition: Informal: a male friend, companion, or member of a group.
examples: He went fishing with the boys.
The boys met after work for dinner.
He has known those boys since childhood.

senses.definition: Historically or offensively: a form of address for an adult man that treats him as inferior, immature, or subordinate.
examples: The term was historically used to demean adult Black men.
He objected to being addressed as 'boy' by the supervisor.
In that historical context, the word carried a deliberately insulting racial meaning.

boyfriend.etymology: Formed from boy and friend. The modern romantic sense developed from the broader idea of a male friend into a term for a male romantic partner.
boyfriend.explanation: Refers to a male romantic partner, especially one with whom a person is dating or in a nonmarital romantic relationship. The term is commonly used for relationships at many ages, despite the word boy in the compound.
usageNotes: Boyfriend most commonly means a male romantic partner rather than simply a male friend.
For adult relationships, boyfriend remains common, although partner may be preferred when a more neutral or formal term is desired.

senses.definition: A male romantic partner in a dating or nonmarital relationship.
examples: She introduced her boyfriend to her family.
Her boyfriend joined them for dinner.
They have been boyfriend and girlfriend for several months.

senses.definition: A man or boy with whom someone has an ongoing romantic relationship.
examples: Her high school boyfriend moved to another city.
She and her boyfriend planned a weekend trip.
He was her first serious boyfriend.

boycott.etymology: Named after Charles Cunningham Boycott, a British land agent in Ireland who was socially and economically isolated in 1880 after a dispute with tenant farmers. His surname soon became a general term for organized refusal to deal with a person, organization, or business.
boycott.explanation: As a verb, boycott means to refuse deliberately to buy from, use, participate in, or otherwise deal with a person, organization, business, product, or event as a form of protest or pressure. As a noun, a boycott is an organized or deliberate refusal of this kind.

senses.definition: Verb: to refuse deliberately to buy, use, attend, support, or deal with something as a form of protest or pressure.
examples: Consumers threatened to boycott the company.
Students voted to boycott the event.
The group urged its members to boycott products made by the manufacturer.

senses.definition: Verb: to refuse social, political, economic, or professional cooperation with a person, organization, or institution.
examples: Several organizations boycotted the negotiations.
Opposition parties decided to boycott the election.
The workers boycotted meetings with the disputed representative.

senses.definition: Noun: an organized refusal to buy, use, attend, support, or participate in something in order to express opposition or exert pressure.
examples: The activists organized a boycott of the store.
The boycott continued for several months.
A consumer boycott reduced sales significantly.

senses.definition: Noun: a deliberate refusal to participate in or cooperate with a person, group, institution, event, or process.
examples: The political parties announced a boycott of the talks.
The athletes considered a boycott of the tournament.
The protest included a nationwide boycott.

brace.etymology: From Old French brace, meaning the two arms, from Latin bracchia, the plural of bracchium, meaning arm. The word later developed senses involving pairs, supports, and structures that hold or strengthen something.
brace.explanation: As a noun, brace can refer to a device that supports, strengthens, aligns, or holds part of the body or another structure in position. It can also mean one of a pair of punctuation marks or, traditionally, a pair of certain animals or objects. As a verb, brace means to support or strengthen something, steady oneself, or prepare mentally or physically for something difficult or forceful.

relatedWords.relationship: Plural noun and common term for orthodontic appliances

senses.definition: Noun: a device or structure used to support, strengthen, align, or hold something in position.
examples: The carpenter added a brace to strengthen the frame.
He wore a knee brace after the injury.
A metal brace supported the damaged shelf.

senses.definition: Noun: an orthodontic device used to straighten or align teeth, usually in the plural form braces.
examples: She wore braces for two years.
The orthodontist adjusted his braces.
Her teeth became straighter after the braces were removed.

senses.definition: Noun: either of a pair of punctuation marks, { }, used to group or enclose information, especially in mathematics, programming, and technical writing.
examples: The programmer forgot to close the final brace.
Place the expression inside braces.
The code block begins with an opening brace.

senses.definition: Noun, traditional: a pair of similar animals or objects, especially game birds.
examples: The hunter returned with a brace of pheasants.
The painting showed a brace of hunting dogs.
The old account mentioned a brace of birds.

senses.definition: Verb: to support, strengthen, or hold something firmly in position.
examples: Workers braced the wall with wooden beams.
She braced the shelf against the frame.
The structure was braced to withstand strong winds.

senses.definition: Verb: to steady or position oneself against movement, force, or impact.
examples: He braced himself against the railing.
Passengers braced themselves as the vehicle stopped suddenly.
She planted her feet and braced for the impact.

senses.definition: Verb: to prepare mentally or emotionally for something difficult, unpleasant, or surprising.
examples: They braced themselves for bad news.
Residents braced for another winter storm.
She braced herself before opening the letter.

bracelet.etymology: From Old French bracelet, a diminutive of bras, meaning arm, ultimately from Latin bracchium, meaning arm
bracelet.explanation: Refers to a piece of jewelry or decorative band worn around the wrist or lower arm. Bracelets may be made from metal, leather, beads, fabric, plastic, or other materials and can be worn for decoration, identification, symbolism, or practical purposes.

senses.definition: A piece of jewelry or decorative band worn around the wrist or lower arm.
examples: She wore a silver bracelet on her wrist.
The bracelet was decorated with small blue stones.
He gave her a bracelet for her birthday.

senses.definition: A band worn around the wrist for identification, access, monitoring, or another practical purpose.
examples: The hospital placed an identification bracelet on the patient.
Visitors received colored bracelets at the entrance.
The fitness bracelet tracks daily activity.

bracket.etymology: From French braguette and later forms referring to a projecting support or architectural brace. The word later developed meanings for punctuation marks and for groups or ranges treated together.
bracket.explanation: Refers to a support attached to a wall or other surface, a punctuation mark used to enclose information, or a category or range into which something is placed. In competitions, a bracket is a diagram showing how participants advance through rounds. As a verb, bracket means to group things together, place them within a range, or enclose material with brackets.

senses.definition: Noun: a projecting support attached to a wall, shelf, beam, or other structure.
examples: The shelf was supported by two metal brackets.
He attached the bracket securely to the wall.
A decorative wooden bracket supported the roof overhang.

senses.definition: Noun: a punctuation mark used to enclose, group, clarify, or separate information.
examples: The editor placed the added explanation in brackets.
The mathematical expression contains several sets of brackets.
Use brackets to identify the material added to the quotation.

senses.definition: Noun: a category, range, or division defined by particular limits, especially for income, age, price, or tax rates.
examples: Their income places them in a higher tax bracket.
The competition has separate age brackets.
The product falls into the middle price bracket.

senses.definition: Noun: a diagram showing the arrangement and progression of competitors through the rounds of a tournament.
examples: The tournament bracket was posted online.
Their team advanced to the next round of the bracket.
Fans filled out brackets before the basketball tournament began.

senses.definition: Verb: to group, classify, or consider two or more people or things together.
examples: Critics often bracket the two writers together.
The study brackets participants according to age.
The products were bracketed into three price ranges.

senses.definition: Verb: to place something between or within two things, limits, or punctuation marks.
examples: The editor bracketed the inserted words.
The estimate was bracketed between two possible values.
Two defensive players bracketed the receiver.

brain.etymology: From Old English brægen, meaning brain, from a Germanic source
brain.explanation: Refers primarily to the organ inside the skull that forms the central part of the nervous system and controls thought, memory, emotion, sensation, movement, and many bodily functions. Figuratively, brain can refer to intelligence, mental ability, or a person regarded as the intellectual force behind an activity or organization.

senses.definition: Noun: the organ inside the skull that controls and coordinates the nervous system, thought, sensation, movement, memory, and many bodily processes.
examples: The human brain contains billions of nerve cells.
The injury affected a small region of the brain.
The brain receives information from the body's sensory organs.

senses.definition: Noun: the mind, intelligence, or ability to think, understand, learn, and solve problems.
examples: The puzzle requires both patience and brain power.
Use your brain before making a decision.
She has a remarkable brain for mathematics.

senses.definition: Noun: a highly intelligent or knowledgeable person.
examples: She is one of the best brains in the department.
The project brought together some of the country's leading scientific brains.
He was regarded as a brilliant legal brain.

senses.definition: Noun: the person who plans, directs, or provides the main ideas behind an activity, project, or organization.
examples: She was the brain behind the successful campaign.
Investigators tried to identify the brain behind the scheme.
He is widely regarded as the creative brain behind the company.

senses.definition: Verb, informal: to strike someone forcefully on the head.
examples: The falling object nearly brained him.
He joked that the low doorway would brain anyone who forgot to duck.
The heavy branch could have brained someone standing beneath it.

brake.etymology: The mechanical sense developed from earlier Germanic words associated with breaking, crushing, or restraining movement. The modern word came to refer to a device used to slow or stop a moving vehicle or machine.
brake.explanation: Refers primarily to a device or system used to slow, stop, or prevent the movement of a vehicle, machine, or rotating part. As a verb, brake means to apply such a device in order to reduce speed or stop. Figuratively, something that acts as a brake can restrain, slow, or limit development or activity.
usageNotes: Brake and break are homophones in most varieties of English but have different meanings and spellings. Brake usually concerns slowing or stopping motion, while break commonly means to damage, separate, interrupt, or violate something.

senses.definition: Noun: a device or system used to slow or stop the movement of a vehicle, machine, wheel, or other moving part.
examples: She pressed the brake to stop the car.
The mechanic replaced the worn brakes.
The bicycle has a brake on each wheel.

senses.definition: Noun: a control used to operate a braking system.
examples: He stepped firmly on the brake.
The driver released the brake before moving forward.
She pulled the emergency brake.

senses.definition: Noun, figurative: something that slows, restrains, or limits progress, growth, or activity.
examples: High borrowing costs acted as a brake on economic growth.
The regulation placed a brake on rapid expansion.
Limited funding became a brake on the project's development.

senses.definition: Verb: to slow or stop a vehicle, machine, or moving object by applying a brake.
examples: The driver braked suddenly to avoid the animal.
She braked before entering the sharp curve.
The cyclist braked at the intersection.

senses.definition: Verb: to reduce the speed or movement of something.
examples: The pilot braked the aircraft after landing.
The system automatically brakes the wheels when slipping is detected.
He braked the cart before it reached the slope.

branch.etymology: From Old French branche, meaning a limb or branch of a tree, ultimately from Late Latin branca, meaning paw, claw, or projecting limb
branch.explanation: Refers primarily to a woody part of a tree that grows outward from the trunk or from another branch. It can also mean a division or subdivision of an organization, field of study, government, family, road, river, or other larger system. As a verb, branch means to divide, spread, or extend into separate parts or directions.

senses.definition: Noun: a woody part of a tree that grows outward from the trunk or from another branch.
examples: A bird landed on the tree branch.
The storm broke several large branches.
Leaves covered every branch of the oak tree.

senses.definition: Noun: a local office, store, or division belonging to a larger organization or business.
examples: The bank opened a new branch downtown.
She works at the company's Seattle branch.
The library system operates several neighborhood branches.

senses.definition: Noun: a major division of a government, institution, organization, or system.
examples: The judicial branch interprets the law.
The organization has separate administrative and educational branches.
Each branch of the military has its own responsibilities.

senses.definition: Noun: a specialized division or field within a larger subject or area of knowledge.
examples: Genetics is a branch of biology.
She studies a branch of mathematics called topology.
Linguistics contains several major branches.

senses.definition: Noun: a line of descent or subdivision within a family, group, or historical tradition.
examples: He belongs to a different branch of the family.
The two branches of the dynasty developed separately.
Researchers traced this branch of the family tree back several centuries.

senses.definition: Noun: a smaller road, river, railway line, or other route that divides from a main one.
examples: The trail follows a branch of the river.
A branch road leads to the village.
The railway branch connects the town with the main line.

senses.definition: Verb: to divide, spread, or extend into separate parts or directions.
examples: The road branches just beyond the bridge.
The river branches into several smaller channels.
The tree branches widely near the top.

senses.definition: Verb: to expand into a new activity, field, product, or area of operation.
examples: The company branched into online publishing.
She decided to branch out into a new area of research.
The restaurant later branched into catering.

brand.etymology: From Old English brand, meaning a burning piece of wood or fire. The word later came to mean a mark made by burning, especially on livestock, and eventually developed the modern commercial sense of a distinctive name, symbol, or identity associated with a product or organization.
brand.explanation: Refers to a name, symbol, design, reputation, or other identity that distinguishes a company, product, service, or organization from others. It can also mean a particular type or variety of something. Historically, a brand was a mark burned onto an animal or object to show ownership. As a verb, brand means to mark, identify, promote, or characterize someone or something in a particular way.

senses.definition: Noun: a name, symbol, design, or other identity used to distinguish a company, product, or service from competitors.
examples: The company launched a new clothing brand.
Customers often recognize the brand by its logo.
The business spent years building a strong brand.

senses.definition: Noun: a particular type, make, or variety of a product.
examples: Which brand of coffee do you prefer?
She switched to a different brand of toothpaste.
The store carries several brands of computer equipment.

senses.definition: Noun: the public image, reputation, or identity associated with a person, company, organization, or product.
examples: The campaign helped strengthen the company's brand.
Her personal brand emphasizes professionalism and reliability.
The scandal damaged the organization's brand.

senses.definition: Noun: a permanent mark traditionally burned onto the skin of livestock or another surface to identify ownership.
examples: The rancher used a distinctive brand on the cattle.
The animal's brand identified the ranch that owned it.
Historic brands were often registered with local authorities.

senses.definition: Verb: to give a product, company, organization, or person a distinctive identity, image, or name.
examples: The company branded the new product for younger consumers.
They branded the service as a premium option.
The organization carefully branded its educational programs.

senses.definition: Verb: to mark an animal or object with a permanent identifying mark, traditionally by burning.
examples: The ranchers branded the cattle for identification.
Each animal was branded with the ranch symbol.
The practice of branding livestock has a long history.

senses.definition: Verb: to publicly describe, label, or characterize someone or something in a particular way, often negatively.
examples: Critics branded the proposal unrealistic.
He was unfairly branded a troublemaker.
The newspaper branded the policy a failure.

brass.etymology: From Old English bræs, meaning brass or a similar metal alloy, from a Germanic source of uncertain origin
brass.explanation: Refers primarily to a yellowish metal alloy made mainly from copper and zinc. Brass is used in musical instruments, hardware, decorations, plumbing, machinery, and many other products. The word can also refer collectively to brass musical instruments or, informally, to high-ranking officials or leaders.
usageNotes: In music, the brass refers collectively to instruments such as trumpets, trombones, French horns, and tubas.
In informal expressions such as 'the top brass,' brass can refer to senior officials, executives, or military officers.

senses.definition: Noun: a yellowish metal alloy made primarily from copper and zinc.
examples: The handle was made of polished brass.
Brass is commonly used for decorative hardware.
The old lamp had a heavy brass base.

senses.definition: Adjective: made of, containing, or resembling brass.
examples: The door has a brass knob.
She polished the brass fittings.
A brass plaque was mounted beside the entrance.

senses.definition: Noun: brass musical instruments considered collectively.
examples: The brass entered during the final section of the composition.
The orchestra's brass played with great power.
He writes music especially well for brass.

senses.definition: Noun: an object, fitting, ornament, or household item made of brass, especially when considered collectively.
examples: She spent the afternoon polishing the brass.
The antique shop displayed old brass and copperware.
The ship's brass was kept brightly polished.

senses.definition: Noun, informal: high-ranking officials, executives, or military officers, especially in the expression 'top brass.'
examples: The top brass attended the strategy meeting.
The proposal required approval from senior brass.
Military brass gathered for the briefing.

brave.etymology: From French brave, meaning courageous, splendid, or fine, ultimately from Italian bravo, meaning bold, courageous, or excellent
brave.explanation: Describes someone who shows courage in the face of danger, fear, difficulty, or pain. It can also describe an action that requires courage. As a verb, brave means to face or endure something difficult or dangerous with courage. As a noun, brave is an older or literary term for a courageous person and has also been used historically for a Native American warrior, a usage that can be dated or stereotypical.
usageNotes: Brave usually emphasizes courage despite fear or danger rather than the complete absence of fear.
The noun use of brave for a Native American warrior is historical and can sound dated or stereotypical in modern English; more specific wording is generally preferable.

senses.definition: Adjective: showing courage when facing danger, fear, pain, or difficulty.
examples: The brave firefighter entered the burning building.
She remained brave throughout the difficult treatment.
It was brave of him to speak openly about the problem.

senses.definition: Adjective: requiring or demonstrating courage.
examples: Rescuing the child was a brave act.
She made a brave decision to challenge the unfair rule.
The soldiers made a brave attempt to defend the position.

senses.definition: Verb: to face, endure, or confront something difficult, dangerous, or unpleasant with courage.
examples: They braved the storm to reach the shelter.
Thousands of people braved the cold to attend the event.
She braved criticism to defend her position.

senses.definition: Noun, literary or historical: a courageous person or warrior.
examples: The poem celebrates the braves who defended their homeland.
The story portrays him as a brave among his people.
Older accounts sometimes used brave as a noun for a warrior.

bravery.etymology: Formed from brave with the noun-forming suffix -ery, referring to the quality or state of being brave
bravery.explanation: Refers to the quality of showing courage when facing danger, fear, pain, hardship, or uncertainty. Bravery does not necessarily mean having no fear; it often means acting with courage despite fear or risk.

senses.definition: The quality of showing courage when facing danger, fear, pain, or difficulty.
examples: The firefighter was honored for his bravery.
She showed remarkable bravery during the emergency.
Their bravery helped protect others from harm.

senses.definition: Courageous behavior or action in a difficult or threatening situation.
examples: His bravery in confronting the problem inspired the entire team.
The rescue required great bravery.
Her bravery in speaking publicly about the injustice earned widespread respect.

breach.etymology: From Middle English breche, from Old English forms related to break, originally referring to a breaking, fracture, or opening made by force
breach.explanation: Refers to a violation of a law, agreement, duty, trust, or security system, or to a gap or opening created by breaking through a barrier. As a verb, breach means to violate an obligation, penetrate or break through a defense or barrier, or compromise a protected system. In descriptions of whales and some other marine animals, breach means to leap partly or completely out of the water.

senses.definition: Noun: a violation or failure to obey a law, agreement, duty, rule, or obligation.
examples: The company was sued for breach of contract.
Officials determined that the disclosure was a breach of policy.
Failure to make the required payment constituted a breach of the agreement.

senses.definition: Noun: a loss or violation of trust, confidence, or proper conduct.
examples: Revealing the private conversation was a serious breach of trust.
The incident created a breach between the two longtime allies.
The unauthorized disclosure was considered a breach of confidentiality.

senses.definition: Noun: a gap, opening, or break made in a wall, barrier, defense, or other protective structure.
examples: The explosion created a breach in the wall.
Soldiers entered through a breach in the defensive line.
Workers repaired the breach in the flood barrier.

senses.definition: Noun: an incident in which protected information, computer systems, or security measures are accessed or compromised without authorization.
examples: The company reported a major data breach.
The security breach exposed thousands of customer records.
Investigators worked to determine how the breach occurred.

senses.definition: Verb: to violate or fail to comply with a law, agreement, duty, rule, or obligation.
examples: The contractor breached the terms of the agreement.
Publishing the information could breach confidentiality rules.
The company was accused of breaching its legal obligations.

senses.definition: Verb: to break through, penetrate, or create an opening in a barrier, defense, or protected area.
examples: The floodwaters breached the levee.
Attackers breached the outer defenses.
The animal breached the fence and escaped.

senses.definition: Verb: to overcome or compromise a security system or protected computer network.
examples: Hackers breached the company's network.
The attackers attempted to breach the security system.
Investigators found that several accounts had been breached.

senses.definition: Verb: for a whale or other marine animal to leap partly or completely out of the water.
examples: A humpback whale breached beside the boat.
Visitors watched as several whales breached offshore.
The whale breached and crashed back into the sea.

bread.etymology: From Old English bread, meaning a piece, morsel, or bread, from a Germanic source
bread.explanation: Refers primarily to a staple food made from flour and liquid, usually combined with yeast or another leavening agent and baked. Bread occurs in many forms, including loaves, rolls, flatbreads, and unleavened varieties. Informally, bread can also mean money or livelihood.
usageNotes: Bread is usually an uncountable noun when referring to the food generally. Individual units are commonly expressed as 'a loaf of bread,' 'a slice of bread,' or 'a piece of bread.'
In informal slang, bread can mean money.

senses.definition: A food made primarily from flour and liquid, usually formed into dough and baked.
examples: She bought fresh bread from the bakery.
He served warm bread with the soup.
The kitchen smelled of freshly baked bread.

senses.definition: A particular type or variety of bread.
examples: The bakery sells several breads made from whole grains.
Rye bread has a distinctive flavor.
They served flatbread alongside the meal.

senses.definition: Food or basic sustenance, especially in figurative or traditional expressions.
examples: For centuries, bread was a basic part of the local diet.
The phrase 'daily bread' can refer broadly to basic necessities.
The work provided bread for the family.

senses.definition: Informal: money, especially money earned for living expenses.
examples: He took the extra job to earn more bread.
The slang term bread has long been used for money.
They were looking for a way to make some extra bread.

breadth.etymology: Formed from broad with the noun-forming suffix -th, following an older pattern in English that also produced words such as length, strength, and width
breadth.explanation: Refers literally to the width of something from one side to another. Figuratively, breadth describes the range, scope, variety, or extent of knowledge, experience, activity, or influence.

senses.definition: The distance or measurement from one side of something to the other; width.
examples: The breadth of the table is nearly three feet.
They measured the length and breadth of the room.
The bridge spans the entire breadth of the river.

senses.definition: The range, scope, or variety covered by a subject, activity, collection, or experience.
examples: The course is impressive in the breadth of topics it covers.
Her research demonstrates considerable breadth.
The museum is known for the breadth of its collection.

senses.definition: The extent or range of a person's knowledge, abilities, interests, or experience.
examples: His breadth of knowledge impressed the committee.
The position requires both depth and breadth of experience.
She developed greater intellectual breadth through extensive reading.

break.etymology: From Old English brecan, meaning to break, shatter, violate, or destroy, from a Germanic source
break.explanation: As a verb, break means to damage, separate, interrupt, violate, or cause something to stop functioning. It can also mean to escape, exceed a limit or record, reveal information, or suddenly begin an action or condition. As a noun, a break can be a fracture, interruption, pause, opening, opportunity, or sudden change.
usageNotes: Break is an irregular verb. Its past tense is broke, and its past participle is broken.

Break and brake are homophones in most varieties of English but have different meanings. Break generally concerns damage, separation, interruption, or violation, while brake refers to slowing or stopping motion.

senses.definition: Verb: to separate, crack, fracture, or damage something into pieces or so that it no longer remains whole.
examples: She accidentally broke the glass.
The branch broke under the weight of the snow.
He fell and broke his arm.

senses.definition: Verb: to cause a machine, device, system, or object to stop working properly.
examples: Dropping the phone could break it.
The power surge broke several pieces of equipment.
He worried that forcing the handle would break the lock.

senses.definition: Verb: to interrupt, stop, or bring an activity, pattern, period, or continuity to an end.
examples: A loud noise broke the silence.
The announcement broke their concentration.
She took a walk to break the routine.

senses.definition: Verb: to violate or fail to obey a law, rule, agreement, promise, or obligation.
examples: He was fined for breaking the law.
The company broke the terms of the contract.
She promised that she would never break her word.

senses.definition: Verb: to exceed, surpass, or set a record, limit, or threshold.
examples: The runner broke the world record.
Temperatures broke previous records during the heat wave.
Sales broke the one-million-dollar mark.

senses.definition: Verb: to escape from confinement, control, or restraint.
examples: The prisoner tried to break free.
The horse broke loose from the fence.
Several animals broke out of the enclosure.

senses.definition: Verb: to reveal, announce, or make information or news publicly known.
examples: The newspaper broke the story early in the morning.
She gently broke the news to her family.
The reporter was the first to break the story.

senses.definition: Noun: a crack, fracture, or damaged place where something has separated.
examples: The X-ray revealed a clean break in the bone.
Workers found a break in the water pipe.
The cable had a break near the connector.

senses.definition: Noun: a temporary pause or interruption in work, activity, travel, or another process.
examples: We took a short break after lunch.
The meeting continued after a ten-minute break.
She needs a break from studying.

senses.definition: Noun: a favorable opportunity, advantage, or piece of good fortune.
examples: The young actor finally got his big break.
She was waiting for a break in her career.
Winning the contract gave the company an important break.

senses.definition: Noun: an interruption, opening, or gap in something continuous.
examples: A break in the clouds revealed the sun.
They waited for a break in traffic before crossing.
There was a brief break in the rain.

breakdown.etymology: Formed from the phrasal verb break down, referring originally to something becoming damaged, collapsing, or ceasing to function. The noun later developed broader senses involving failure, analysis, division, and loss of physical or emotional stability.
breakdown.explanation: Refers to a failure, collapse, or loss of normal functioning in a machine, system, relationship, process, or person. It can also mean a detailed analysis or division of something into smaller parts, categories, or components.
usageNotes: Breakdown is normally written as one word when it is a noun. The corresponding phrasal verb is written as two words: break down.
A breakdown can refer to mechanical failure, failure of communication or organization, physical or emotional collapse, or a detailed analysis of information.

senses.definition: A mechanical or technical failure that causes a machine, vehicle, or system to stop functioning properly.
examples: The car suffered a breakdown on the highway.
A mechanical breakdown delayed production.
The technician investigated the equipment breakdown.

senses.definition: A failure or collapse of a system, process, relationship, agreement, or organization.
examples: The dispute led to a breakdown in negotiations.
A breakdown in communication caused several mistakes.
The crisis exposed a serious breakdown of administrative procedures.

senses.definition: A detailed analysis, explanation, or division of something into smaller parts, categories, or components.
examples: The report provides a breakdown of annual expenses.
She requested a detailed breakdown of the survey results.
The chart shows the population breakdown by age group.

senses.definition: A serious loss of emotional or psychological stability that makes normal functioning difficult.
examples: The prolonged stress contributed to an emotional breakdown.
He took time away from work after the breakdown.
The character experiences a psychological breakdown near the end of the novel.

senses.definition: The physical decomposition, separation, or deterioration of a substance or material into smaller or simpler parts.
examples: The breakdown of organic matter releases nutrients into the soil.
Enzymes assist in the breakdown of food during digestion.
Scientists studied the chemical breakdown of the material.

breakfast.etymology: Formed from break and fast, originally referring to the meal that breaks the period of fasting that occurs overnight
breakfast.explanation: Refers to the first meal of the day, usually eaten in the morning after waking. As a verb, breakfast means to eat breakfast or to provide someone with breakfast.

senses.definition: Noun: the first meal of the day, usually eaten in the morning.
examples: She ate cereal and fruit for breakfast.
Breakfast is served from seven until ten.
He skipped breakfast because he was in a hurry.

senses.definition: Noun: the food prepared or eaten as the first meal of the day.
examples: The hotel provides a free breakfast.
They prepared a large breakfast for the guests.
Breakfast included eggs, toast, and fresh fruit.

senses.definition: Verb: to eat the first meal of the day.
examples: They breakfasted together before leaving.
We breakfasted early and began the journey.
She usually breakfasts at home.

senses.definition: Verb: to provide someone with breakfast.
examples: The inn breakfasted its guests before sunrise.
They breakfasted the travelers before sending them on their way.
The hosts breakfasted the group in the main dining room.

breakthrough.etymology: Formed from the phrasal verb break through, originally referring to penetrating or passing through a barrier or defensive line. The noun later developed a figurative sense for an important advance, discovery, or achievement.
breakthrough.explanation: Refers to an important discovery, achievement, or advance that overcomes a major difficulty or creates new possibilities. It can also mean the successful penetration of a physical or military barrier. As an adjective, breakthrough describes a development, technology, treatment, or achievement that represents a major advance.
usageNotes: Breakthrough is normally written as one word when used as a noun or adjective. The corresponding phrasal verb is written as two words: break through.
A breakthrough usually implies overcoming an important obstacle or making progress after a period of difficulty or uncertainty.

senses.definition: Noun: an important discovery, achievement, or advance that overcomes a major obstacle or significantly improves understanding.
examples: Scientists announced a major breakthrough in cancer research.
The discovery represented an important technological breakthrough.
Years of experimentation finally produced a breakthrough.

senses.definition: Noun: a sudden or significant improvement in a difficult situation, negotiation, relationship, or problem.
examples: The negotiations produced a breakthrough after weeks of disagreement.
Therapy helped him achieve an emotional breakthrough.
Diplomats hoped the meeting would lead to a breakthrough in the dispute.

senses.definition: Noun: the successful penetration or passage through a barrier, defensive line, or other obstruction.
examples: The troops achieved a breakthrough in the defensive line.
The offensive created a narrow breakthrough near the border.
Commanders attempted to exploit the breakthrough before the defenses could recover.

senses.definition: Adjective: representing or involving a major advance, discovery, or achievement.
examples: Researchers developed a breakthrough treatment for the disease.
The company introduced breakthrough technology for storing energy.
Her breakthrough performance brought her international recognition.

breast.etymology: From Old English breost, meaning breast or chest, from a Germanic source
breast.explanation: Refers primarily to either of the two mammary structures on the chest of a human, especially a woman, or to the corresponding front chest area of certain animals. It can also refer to breast meat from poultry or to the front part of the body or an object. As a verb, breast can mean to move against or overcome something directly, especially a hill, wave, or obstacle.

senses.definition: Noun: either of the two mammary structures located on the front of the human chest, especially in women.
examples: The doctor examined the patient's breast.
Breast tissue changes during pregnancy.
She scheduled a routine breast examination.

senses.definition: Noun: the front part of the chest of a person, bird, or other animal.
examples: The bird has bright red feathers on its breast.
He placed his hand against his breast.
The animal's breast was covered with thick fur.

senses.definition: Noun: meat taken from the breast or chest portion of poultry or another animal.
examples: She ordered grilled chicken breast.
The recipe calls for two turkey breasts.
He sliced the roasted breast before serving it.

senses.definition: Noun: the front or forward-facing part of something, especially when compared with the chest of a body.
examples: The breast of the wave rose sharply ahead of the boat.
The climber reached the breast of the hill.
The structure projected from the breast of the slope.

senses.definition: Verb: to move against, face, or overcome something directly, especially a hill, wave, or other obstacle.
examples: The hikers breasted the hill before sunset.
The boat breasted the waves during the storm.
She breasted the final rise and saw the valley below.

breath.etymology: From Old English bræth, meaning breath, vapor, odor, or exhalation, from a Germanic source
breath.explanation: Refers to the air taken into or expelled from the lungs during breathing, or to a single act or cycle of breathing. It can also refer figuratively to a brief pause, a slight movement of air, or a small indication of a quality, feeling, or idea.
usageNotes: Breath is a noun and is pronounced BRETH. Breathe is the related verb and is pronounced BREETH.
The plural of breath is breaths.

senses.definition: The air taken into or expelled from the lungs during breathing.
examples: Her breath was visible in the cold air.
He could feel the warmth of his breath on his hands.
The doctor listened as she took a deep breath.

senses.definition: A single inhalation or exhalation, or one cycle of breathing.
examples: Take a slow, deep breath.
He held his breath underwater.
She paused for a breath before continuing.

senses.definition: The ability or capacity to breathe.
examples: The runner struggled to catch his breath.
The steep climb left her short of breath.
He stopped briefly to get his breath back.

senses.definition: A brief pause or short period of rest.
examples: The workers took a moment to catch their breath.
The quiet weekend gave everyone a little breathing space and a breath from the usual routine.
After finishing the first task, she allowed herself a brief breath before starting the next.

senses.definition: A slight movement or current of air.
examples: A breath of wind moved through the trees.
There was hardly a breath of air in the room.
A cool breath from the open window crossed the room.

senses.definition: A slight trace, suggestion, or indication of a quality, feeling, or idea.
examples: There was a breath of optimism in his remarks.
The design adds a breath of modern style to the old building.
Her voice contained a faint breath of disappointment.

breathe.etymology: From Middle English brethen, formed from breath and ultimately related to Old English words referring to breathing, vapor, and exhalation
breathe.explanation: Means to take air into the lungs and release it again. It can also mean to inhale or exhale a particular substance, to allow air or moisture to pass through a material, or figuratively to express, suggest, or give life to a particular quality or feeling.
usageNotes: Breathe is a verb and is pronounced BREETH. Breath is the related noun and is pronounced BRETH.
The past tense and past participle of breathe are both breathed.

senses.definition: To take air into the lungs and release it again.
examples: She breathed slowly and deeply.
Humans need oxygen in order to breathe.
He found it difficult to breathe after running.

senses.definition: To inhale or exhale a particular gas, vapor, odor, or other substance.
examples: The workers wore masks to avoid breathing the fumes.
She breathed in the cool morning air.
He accidentally breathed smoke from the fire.

senses.definition: To allow air, vapor, or moisture to pass through or circulate.
examples: This fabric allows the skin to breathe.
The shoes are designed to breathe during exercise.
Natural materials often breathe better than synthetic ones.

senses.definition: To speak, whisper, or express something very softly.
examples: She breathed his name quietly.
He breathed a warning into her ear.
The actor breathed the final words of the scene.

senses.definition: Figurative: to express, suggest, or seem filled with a particular quality, atmosphere, or feeling.
examples: The old house breathes history.
Her performance breathed confidence and energy.
The garden seemed to breathe peace and quiet.

senses.definition: Figurative: to give life, energy, or renewed vitality to something.
examples: The renovation breathed new life into the neighborhood.
Fresh leadership breathed energy into the organization.
The new design breathed life into an outdated product.

breathtaking.etymology: Formed from breath and taking, based on the figurative idea that something extremely beautiful, surprising, or impressive can seem to take a person's breath away
breathtaking.explanation: Describes something so beautiful, impressive, surprising, exciting, or extreme that it produces a strong emotional reaction. It is especially common for spectacular scenery, artistic performances, dramatic experiences, and unusually great speed, skill, or intensity.
usageNotes: Breathtaking is usually figurative. It generally means extremely beautiful, impressive, surprising, or exciting rather than literally preventing someone from breathing.

senses.definition: Extremely beautiful, impressive, or spectacular.
examples: The mountain offered a breathtaking view of the valley.
They watched a breathtaking sunset over the ocean.
The palace contains several breathtaking works of art.

senses.definition: Extremely exciting, surprising, or emotionally powerful.
examples: The final minutes of the game were breathtaking.
Her performance was absolutely breathtaking.
The rescue involved several breathtaking moments.

senses.definition: Remarkably great, rapid, skillful, or intense in degree.
examples: Technology has advanced at a breathtaking pace.
The driver reached breathtaking speeds on the track.
The gymnast completed the routine with breathtaking skill.

breed.etymology: From Old English bredan, meaning to nourish, raise, bring up, or produce offspring, from a Germanic source
breed.explanation: As a noun, breed refers to a recognized group of domesticated animals that share inherited characteristics produced through ancestry and selective breeding. More broadly, it can describe a type or kind of person or thing. As a verb, breed means to reproduce, to cause animals or plants to reproduce for particular characteristics, to raise animals, or figuratively to cause a condition, attitude, or problem to develop.
usageNotes: Breed is an irregular verb. Its past tense and past participle are both bred.
Breed is most commonly used for recognized varieties of domesticated animals, while species refers to a biological classification involving naturally reproducing populations.

senses.definition: Noun: a recognized group of domesticated animals having distinctive inherited characteristics.
examples: The Labrador Retriever is a popular breed of dog.
Farmers selected a cattle breed suited to the local climate.
The horse belongs to a breed known for its speed.

senses.definition: Noun: a particular type, kind, or category of person or thing.
examples: She represents a new breed of entrepreneur.
The aircraft belongs to a different breed of military technology.
The organization developed a new breed of training program.

senses.definition: Verb: for animals to mate and produce offspring.
examples: The birds breed during the spring.
These frogs breed in shallow ponds.
The animals normally breed once each year.

senses.definition: Verb: to cause animals or plants to reproduce in order to develop or preserve particular characteristics.
examples: The farmer breeds sheep for high-quality wool.
Scientists bred the plants for greater resistance to disease.
The kennel breeds dogs with carefully documented ancestry.

senses.definition: Verb: to raise, develop, or produce animals or plants through reproduction.
examples: The farm breeds horses for racing.
They have bred cattle for several generations.
The nursery breeds new varieties of ornamental plants.

senses.definition: Verb, figurative: to cause a feeling, condition, behavior, or problem to develop or increase.
examples: Secrecy can breed distrust.
Poor sanitation may breed disease.
Continued resentment bred hostility between the two groups.
